title: Training exposure, recovery, and injury incidence among course-based and competitive university Wushu Taolu practitioners: a 12-week prospective cohort study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Whether the large training-exposure difference between course-based and competitive-team university Wushu Taolu practitioners in China translates into a correspondingly different musculoskeletal health burden has not been well characterized prospectively.
METHODS: In this observational, non-randomized cohort study, 255 practitioners (128 course-based, 127 university-team; mean age 20.7 ± 1.5) were followed over four waves (T0-T3) across 12 weeks, with training load, sleep, recovery, health problems, and injury recorded using recall windows matched to each variable's time-scale.
RESULTS: University-team practitioners had substantially higher training exposure than course-based practitioners. The 12-week cumulative incidence of new injury was substantially higher in university-team practitioners than in course-based practitioners (68.9% vs. 20.0%; p < 0.001), with higher adjusted odds of injury (OR = 6.31, 95% CI 1.49-26.69). However, when injury occurrence was expressed relative to estimated training exposure, the between-group difference was much smaller: 10.56 versus 8.98 positive new-injury person-wave observations per 1,000 estimated training hours, respectively (IRR = 1.18, 95% CI 0.79-1.75). Prior injury within the preceding 12 months was strongly associated with subsequent injury (OR = 4.06, 95% CI 2.03-8.13).
CONCLUSION: University-team practitioners experienced a substantially greater absolute injury burden than course-based practitioners, whereas the between-group difference was much smaller when injury occurrence was expressed relative to estimated training exposure. Prior injury history was a strong marker of subsequent injury. Because group membership and training exposure were highly correlated and the study was observational, these findings should not be interpreted causally.

title: Neurophysiological and neuromuscular responses associated with the repeated bout effect following eccentric exercise in healthy adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Muscle damage severity decreases after repeated eccentric exercise bouts (the repeated bout effect [RBE]), but whether accompanying neural and neuromuscular changes contribute to protection or arise secondary to reduced damage remains unclear. This systematic review and meta-analysis compared neurophysiological and neuromuscular responses between initial and repeated eccentric bouts in healthy adults. Eight databases were searched from November 1990 to January 2025, and Hedges' g was calculated where outcomes were comparable. Given the small number of contributing studies, all pooled analyses were considered exploratory. Twelve studies met the inclusion criteria. Twitch/evoked force showed recovery-compatible point estimates at 24 h (g = 1.02, 95% CI -0.03-2.06) and 48 h (g = 0.50, 95% CI 0.08-0.92). Voluntary activation findings were mixed. TMS-derived voluntary activation produced positive single-study estimates at 24 h (g = 1.10, 95% CI 0.29-1.92) and 48 h (g = 1.06, 95% CI 0.26-1.87), whereas pooled ITT-derived estimates were imprecise at 24 h (g = 0.36, 95% CI -0.92-1.63) and recovery-compatible but based on only two studies at 48 h (g = 0.44, 95% CI 0.03-0.85). M-wave/Mmax showed no consistent between-bout pattern. Corticospinal, intracortical, spinal, reticulospinal, motor-unit and EMG findings were limited, inconsistent or directionally unclear. Neural and neuromuscular changes accompany the RBE, but whether they contribute to protection or reflect reduced damage remains unresolved. Peripheral contractile outcomes showed the most consistent recovery-compatible pattern, whereas evidence concerning central activation and motor-unit behaviour remained limited or inconsistent.

title: Development of Physical Fitness in Young Athletes: A Longitudinal Meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Understanding how physical fitness develops during adolescence is critical for interpreting and optimizing training and setting realistic performance expectations in youth sport. Yet, evidence-based, age-referenced benchmarks that track multiple fitness components across sports remain lacking, leaving practitioners without reliable normative trajectories to guide athlete development.
PURPOSE: This longitudinal meta-analysis estimated developmental trajectories for vertical jump, sprint, and endurance performance in male youth athletes across multiple sports using data from longitudinal studies.
METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, we conducted a systematic search of MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Scopus for studies with repeated measurements of vertical jump, 10-meter sprint, and endurance performance in male youth athletes, from database inception to October 4, 2025. Analyses were restricted to males due to an insufficient number of eligible studies including female athletes. We applied a risk-of-bias assessment adapted from the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool and examined publication bias through funnel plot inspection and Egger's regression test. We used Bayesian multilevel growth curve modeling to estimate age-related developmental trajectories, with analyses stratified by sport and test protocol.
RESULTS: Twenty-eight studies met eligibility criteria, providing 41 independent samples across nine sports. Vertical jump and endurance performance exhibited curvilinear trajectories with peak velocity occurring at 13.2 years (68% CrI [±1 posterior SD]: 13.0; 13.5) and 13.8 years (68% CrI: 13.6; 14.2), respectively, overlapping the typical period of peak height velocity in male athletes. Sprint performance showed linear improvement throughout adolescence (ages 12-17) without distinct acceleration periods. Sport-specific analyses revealed varying absolute values but broadly similar developmental patterns within each fitness component, with rugby exhibiting the highest vertical jump values and minimal sport differences observed for sprint development.
CONCLUSION: The present age-referenced trajectories offer practical benchmarks for monitoring progression and setting realistic expectations in youth sport contexts. Our findings reveal distinct developmental patterns-curvilinear trajectories for vertical jump and endurance with peak improvements around ages 13-14 versus linear progression for sprint-with peak velocities coinciding with typical maturation timing Trial registration: CRD42020175084 (PROSPERO) 25/03/2020.

title: Impact of Sprint Duration With Fixed Recovery on Acute Physiological and Performance Responses to Repeated Cycle Sprints in Hypoxia in Male and Female Sprinters.
abstract: Repeated short sprints (≤ 10 s) in hypoxia are often used to enhance performance, but acute responses to longer sprints (> 10 s) performed in a repeated-sprint format with short recovery periods (∼30 s) remain unclear. We examined performance and physiological strain during repeated short (10-s) and long (15-s) sprints with identical recovery (30 s) comparing acute responses between sexes. Sixteen highly trained sprinters (7 females) performed 7 × 10-s (10:30) and 15-s (15:30) sprints with 30-s rest in normobaric hypoxia (FiO2: 0.15), using a randomized cross-over design. Average mean power output across the seven sprints was lower in 15:30 than 10:30 (6.30 ± 0.44 vs. 6.85 ± 0.82 W/kg; p < 0.001). Sprint decrement score (Sdec) was larger in 15:30 than 10:30 (-17.9 ± 4.8% vs. -13.1 ± 4.6%; p < 0.001). Average pulse oximetry-derived peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) across the seven sprints was lower in 15:30 than 10:30 (87.1 ± 4.2% vs. 89.7 ± 2.7%; p < 0.001), whereas the magnitude of change from sprint 1 to sprint 7 did not clearly differ between conditions. Heart rate increased across sprints (Δsprint1-7: +9.2 ± 5.3% and p < 0.001), independently of condition (p = 0.652). ΔSpO2 correlated with ΔSdec (r = 0.609 and p = 0.012). Female athletes experienced smaller performance declines than males in both conditions (p = 0.001). Longer repeated sprints with identical rest in hypoxia impair mechanical output while inducing greater physiological strain, with comparatively smaller performance reductions in females.

title: Patient and healthcare professional perceptions of weight reduction in the treatment of knee osteoarthritis: A systematic literature review.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Weight reduction confers significant clinical benefits in knee osteoarthritis (OA) management. This systematic review examined patients' and healthcare professionals' (HCPs) perceptions of weight reduction for surgical, pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions, with emphasis on barriers to implementation.
METHOD: The review was conducted across Embase, MEDLINE, Cochrane, and PsycInfo for eligible studies using the Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome, Timeframe, and Study type framework.
RESULTS: The search identified 2134 publications; of these, 203 had full-text screening, with 46 studies included: 23 qualitative studies, 15 cross-sectional studies, 6 randomized-controlled trials, one quasi-experimental and one observational cohort study. Four main themes of barriers to weight reduction were identified, including limited knowledge, lack of access to interventions, OA-specific barriers to exercise, and non-OA-specific barriers to dieting and exercise. The patient-reported barriers included intrapersonal barriers (i.e., difficulty achieving weight reduction, lack of motivation), physical barriers (i.e., age, challenges with general movement), and social barriers (i.e., lack of social support). The HCP-reported barriers included knowledge barriers, communication barriers, and systemic barriers (i.e., time constraints and resource limitations). Both patients and HCPs had varying expectations and satisfaction levels regarding the impact and delivery of weight reduction interventions.
CONCLUSIONS: Despite broad recognition of weight reduction's benefits in knee OA, substantial barriers hinder adherence and implementation. Targeted strategies addressing patient-HCP communication, alongside enhanced education and training for both groups, are critical to improving weight reduction outcomes in this population. There is currently a gap in evidence around barriers to gastric surgery and pharmacological treatment specific to patients with knee OA.

title: Is Training Transfer Uniform? A Systematic Review and Three-Level Meta-Analysis of Resisted Sprint Training Effects on Acceleration, Jumping, and Change of Direction Performance in Athletes.
abstract: Resisted sprint training (RST) is widely used to improve acceleration, but transfer to jumping and changing direction remains unclear. This review examined RST effects on acceleration, vertical and horizontal jump, and change of direction performance, with variation by comparator and training characteristics. Eight databases were searched to 7 July 2026. The review included 66 independent studies and 1945 participants; 31 controlled studies contributed 179 effect sizes to the primary analysis. Three-level random-effects models accounted for dependence within studies. RST favored acceleration (g = 0.32, 95% CI [0.16, 0.49]), vertical jump (g = 0.25, 95% CI [0.06, 0.44]), horizontal jump (g = 0.24, 95% CI [0.11, 0.37]), and change of direction performance (g = 0.46, 95% CI [0.09, 0.82]). Prediction intervals crossed zero for acceleration, vertical jump, and change of direction performance, but not horizontal jump. After adjustment for comparator type, effects did not clearly differ among domains (p = 0.699). Compared with unresisted sprint training, additional mean effects were small (g = 0.22-0.30). Exploratory moderator analyses found no clear associations with comparator type, external load, training dose, or RST modality. GRADE certainty was moderate for acceleration and low for other outcomes. RST showed favorable mean effects across all four domains, although benefits in new training contexts remain uncertain. Evidence identifies no universal load, dose, or superior modality, and the predominantly male evidence base limits generalizability to female athletes. RST is best viewed as a targeted overload method complementing sprinting at high speed and training specific to the task.

title: Cardiovascular Effects Associated with the Female Athlete Triad: Emerging Evidence Statement from the Female and Male Athlete Triad Coalition.
abstract: This is an emerging evidence statement from the Female and Male Athlete Triad Coalition. This paper complements the 2025 updates to the Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statements addressing the State of the Science and Clinical Guidelines for Screening, Diagnosis, Treatment and Return to Play. This paper examines emerging evidence of cardiovascular alterations in Triad-affected female athletes with functional hypothalamic amenorrhea and functional hypothalamic oligomenorrhea, including vascular, hemodynamic, autonomic and lipid perturbations. The clinical significance of these surrogate markers of cardiovascular function and their long-term cardiovascular implications remain to be determined. Notwithstanding, the current work extends existing Triad frameworks by recognizing cardiovascular perturbations potentially associated with energy deficiency and hypoestrogenism as an important consideration in female athlete health. We outline an evidence-informed research framework, including longitudinal, dose-response, and multimodal assessments, to characterize the onset, magnitude, physiological significance, and reversibility of cardiovascular alterations in athletes with functional hypothalamic amenorrhea and functional hypothalamic oligomenorrhea. By integrating evidence from sports physiology, endocrinology, and cardiovascular medicine, this state-of-the-science synthesis provides a roadmap for future research, screening, and intervention strategies. It also underscores the importance of evaluating cardiovascular health as a potential component of the broader physiological consequences of energy deficiency, alongside menstrual dysfunction, and impaired bone health.

title: Urinary metabolomic signatures of muscle injury and recovery in elite football players.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Muscle injuries are a leading cause of time-loss in elite football, highlighting the need for objective biomarkers capable of reflecting the athlete's physiological state. Monitoring strategies rely predominantly on external load metrics and may not fully capture internal physiological responses to training and competition. Urinary metabolomics offers a non-invasive approach to characterize injury related physiological processes.
OBJECTIVES: To identify urinary metabolomic signatures associated with muscle injury in elite football players and to explore their potential utility for monitoring injury-related physiological stress and recovery.
METHODS: This observational longitudinal study included 287 urine samples collected from 121 elite male football players across two consecutive seasons. Samples were clinically classified as muscle injury (n = 30) or control (n = 257). Targeted UPLC-MS quantified amino acids and tryptophan-related metabolites. Univariate analysis, pathway over-representation analysis, and PLS-DA were applied to identify injury-associated metabolic patterns RESULTS: Muscle injury was associated with alterations in amino acid turnover, purine metabolism, energetic stress, and tryptophan catabolism. Exploratory pathway analysis suggested enrichment of amino acid-related pathways, although interpretation was limited by the targeted nature of the analytical panel. PLS-DA identified an injury-associated metabolic signature with a cross-validated AUROC of 0.88 (sensitivity 73%, specificity 88%; p < 0.003). Key discriminant metabolites included β-aminoisobutyric acid, hypoxanthine, xanthurenic acid, β-alanine, and alanine. Exploratory visual assessment of individual longitudinal trajectories suggested a return toward baseline during rehabilitation.
CONCLUSIONS: Urinary metabolomics identifies coordinated metabolic alterations associated with muscle injury in elite football players, supporting its potential as a future complementary tool to external load monitoring. Further validation in larger cohorts is required before these systemic signatures can be applied to clinical monitoring or recovery assessment.

title: Dose-dependent effects of sodium bicarbonate supplementation combined with sprint interval training on performance adaptations in basketball players: a randomized placebo-controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sprint interval training (SIT) effectively improves physical performance in team-sport athletes, while sodium bicarbonate (Sb) supplementation may enhance training adaptations. However, the dose-dependent effects of Sb during SIT remain unclear in basketball players. Therefore, this study examined the effects of two Sb doses combined with SIT on physical performance adaptations in basketball players.
METHODS: Forty trained male basketball players (age: 21.6 ± 2.0 years, height: 185.4 ± 3.5 cm, body mass: 84.1 ± 4.4 kg) were recruited and randomly assigned to four groups: SIT + 0.3 g·kg-1 Sb (n = 10), SIT + 0.45 g·kg-1 Sb (n = 10), SIT + placebo (PL) (n = 10), and control (CON) (n = 10). The intervention lasted four weeks during the preparatory phase of the season. Participants in the training groups performed SIT three times per week in addition to their regular basketball training. The SIT protocol consisted of four sets of ten 5-second maximal sprints, with 20 seconds of active recovery between repetitions and 2 minutes of rest between sets. All 40 enrolled participants successfully completed the 4-week intervention, resulting in a 0% dropout rate. Performance assessments conducted before and after the intervention included countermovement vertical jump (CMVJ), standing long jump (SLJ), 20 m sprint, Illinois change-of-direction speed (CODS), Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test Level 1 (Yo-Yo IR1), and Wingate anaerobic power (peak power output [PPO] and mean power output [MPO]).
RESULTS: All training groups showed significant improvements in physical performance variables over time (p < 0.05). Significant group by time interaction effects were observed for all performance variables (p ≤ 0.001), indicating that the SIT groups showed more gains compared with the CON group. Both Sb supplementation groups demonstrated greater improvements than the SIT + PL group in CMVJ, SLJ, sprint performance, CODS, Yo-Yo IR1 distance, PPO, and MPO (p < 0.05). Furthermore, the SIT + 0.45 g·kg-1 Sb group exhibited significantly greater performance enhancements than the SIT + 0.3 g·kg-1 Sb group across all measured variables.
CONCLUSION: Four weeks of SIT improved performance in trained basketball players, with Sb supplementation providing additional dose-dependent benefits (0.45 > 0.3 g⋅kg-1). While the higher dose yielded superior adaptations, its practical application should be balanced against potential gastrointestinal discomfort and individual tolerance to ensure long-term athlete compliance.

title: Screening-based low energy availability risk, disordered eating risk, and their co-occurrence among female volleyball players: a cross-sectional study.
abstract: Low energy availability (LEA) and disordered eating (DE) are important health concerns in female athletes, yet their occurrence and co-occurrence in team-sport contexts, particularly volleyball, remain underexplored. This cross-sectional online survey study examined the proportions of athletes classified as being at risk of LEA and DE overall and across competition levels, and assessed the co-occurrence between the two risk classifications in female volleyball players in Türkiye, using the Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q) and Eating Attitudes Test-26 (EAT-26). It also examined correlations between EAT-26 total score and LEAF-Q total and domain scores. A total of 213 athletes, recruited via non-probability convenience sampling, completed the LEAF-Q and EAT-26 to assess LEA risk and DE risk, respectively. In this sample, 33.3% of athletes were classified as being at risk of LEA, with no difference across competition levels (p = 0.825). A total of 17.4% were classified as being at risk of DE, with variation across competition levels and the highest proportion among Turkish Women's Volleyball Second League athletes (p = 0.034). LEA risk and DE risk co-occurred in 10.3% of the sample, and DE risk was associated with higher odds of LEA risk (unadjusted OR = 3.80, 95% CI: 1.82-7.92). EAT-26 total score was positively correlated with LEAF-Q total and gastrointestinal function scores (p < 0.001) and injury history score (p = 0.004), but not menstrual function score (p = 0.133). These results suggest that LEA risk was commonly identified in this sample, DE risk was comparatively less common, and their co-occurrence was only partial, highlighting the value of screening for both risks rather than assuming one from the other.

title: Calf Injuries: An Anatomy-Based Approach to Diagnosis, Management and Return to Sport.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Calf muscle injuries are common in athletes but represent a heterogeneous group of lesions involving different muscles and myoconnective structures. This review provides a practical overview of gastrocnemius-soleus injuries, with particular emphasis on how anatomical characterization can contribute to diagnosis, management and return-to-sport decision-making. It also examines the limitations of current evidence and the extent to which increasingly detailed imaging findings translate into clinically meaningful information.
RECENT FINDINGS: Advances in ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging have improved the identification of specific injury patterns involving the gastrocnemius and soleus. Recent studies support moving beyond a muscle-based diagnosis towards more precise characterisation of the myoconnective structures involved. However, evidence linking individual anatomical patterns to prognosis and return-to-sport outcomes remains limited and largely observational. Current rehabilitation approaches favour progressive, criteria-based loading rather than fixed timelines, while return-to-sport decisions increasingly integrate clinical recovery, functional capacity, sport-specific demands and acceptable risk. No validated calf-specific rehabilitation or return-to-sport criteria are currently available. Anatomical characterization provides a useful framework for understanding the heterogeneity of calf muscle injuries but should inform rather than determine clinical management. Rehabilitation should remain function-led and progressively restore the mechanical capacities required for sport, while return to sport should be considered a multifactorial decision rather than the result of isolated imaging findings, tests or predefined timelines. Future prospective studies should determine which anatomical features provide clinically relevant prognostic information and develop validated calf-specific functional and return-to-sport outcomes.

title: Perineural Release with or Without Balloon Decompression for the Treatment of Lumbosacral Discogenic Syndromes in Professional Athletes.
abstract: Background: Lumbosacral discogenic syndrome (LSDS) is a common cause of low back pain (LBP) and lower limb pain (LLP) in athletes, often resulting in impaired sporting performance and delayed return to sport (RTS). Evidence regarding minimally invasive interventions, such as epidural perineural release (PNR), remains limited in athletic populations. Aim: This study aimed to compare outcomes following PNR with versus without balloon decompression neuroplasty in athletes with LSDS. Methods: We conducted a retrospective review of PNR performed between 2019 and 2024 for the treatment of LSDS among professional athletes. Demographic, clinical, and outcome data were collected from medical records and follow-up assessments. Pain intensity was assessed using the Numerical Rating Scale (NRS), while patient-reported outcomes were evaluated using the EuroQoL-5D (EQ-5D). Additional outcomes included pain-free walking, standing, and sitting durations, and self-reported health scores. Results: A total of 33 patients who had one intervention were included. Significant improvements were observed in all pain, functional, and quality-of-life outcomes following treatment (all p < 0.001). Maximum, minimum, and average pain intensity decreased from 7.5 ± 1.7 to 2.8 ± 2.2, 3.8 ± 2.3 to 0.3 ± 0.7, and 5.6 ± 1.7 to 1.5 ± 1.2, respectively. All EQ-5D domains and quality of sleep also improved significantly (all p < 0.001). Pain-free walking, standing, and sitting durations increased significantly, from 24.8 ± 23.2 to 49.7 ± 26.7 min, 18.4 ± 20.0 to 44.1 ± 23.1 min, and 25.5 ± 23.7 to 44.6 ± 24.9 min, respectively (all p < 0.001). Self-reported health scores improved from 51.9 ± 22.6 to 83.0 ± 14.3 (p < 0.001). Conclusions: Epidural perineural release, with or without balloon decompression neuroplasty, was associated by significant improvements in pain, functional capacity, and quality of life among athletes with LSDS refractory to conservative management. These findings suggest that PNR may be a promising minimally invasive treatment option; however, controlled prospective studies are required to establish its effectiveness and determine the additional benefit of balloon decompression.

title: The Mum-Alete: An Observational Survey-Based Study of Australian Athletes Returning to High-Performance Sport After Pregnancy.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: As more female athletes extend their careers and resume high-performance sport following childbirth, there is an increasing need to understand factors influencing this transition. The return-to-high-performance sport process for postpartum athletes remains complex, with limited evidence available to guide sporting organisations and practitioners. This study aimed to identify the experiences, facilitators, challenges, and barriers for athletes returning to high-performance sport postpartum.
DESIGN: An exploratory cross-sectional survey study.
METHODS: Participants included postpartum elite and sub-elite Australian athletes who maintained training 6 months prior to conception and gave birth between July 2016 and February 2022. The online Mum-Alete survey included various types of closed-ended questions as well as open-ended questions to gather deeper insights related to demographic/pregnancy information, training and performance, physical health (e.g., sport-related injuries), and social factors impacting return to high-performance sport. Descriptive statistics were used to summarise data, while a hybrid thematic analysis was used for qualitative analyses.
RESULTS: Descriptive analyses for the 64 athletes who participated showed most resumed exercise within 6-week postpartum, with pelvic floor exercises initiated earliest. Endurance and strength training followed, though 59% of respondents reported performance declines and 43% reported sport-related injuries. Key challenges in returning to high-performance sport included time management, sleep, breastfeeding, and pelvic floor dysfunction. Among facilitators in returning to high-performance sport, support from family, coaches, and medical staff was generally rated positively, with many athletes reporting a lack of (or non-awareness of) organisational policies and support provisions (e.g., well-being officer, maternity leave, status protections, including stipends, caregiver allowance to attend training) as well as facility-related challenges (e.g., dedicated spaces for childcare and breastfeeding). Eight qualitative themes were identified, including time/time management, training 'new' bodies, safe return to high-performance sport, breastfeeding while participating, critical support, navigating motherhood and sport, discrimination, and education/expertise.
CONCLUSIONS: This study showed that while athletes returned to high-performance training relatively early following childbirth, they regularly perceived reductions in performance and reported sport-related injuries. Various factors were also shown to facilitate and challenge the return-to-high-performance sport process. These outcomes highlight the need for athlete-informed, multidisciplinary, and flexible support strategies, and underscore critical gaps in organisational practice.

title: A Longitudinal Study Analyzing Sprint Performance in Relation to Biological Maturity in Youth Soccer Players.
abstract: Bezzina, D, Price, P, Cimadoro, G, and Cleather, D. A longitudinal study analyzing sprint performance in relation to biological maturity in youth soccer players. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Understanding the influence of biological maturation on athletic performance is crucial for improving youth training programs. This study examined the longitudinal development of sprint performance in youth soccer players across different stages of biological maturation. Forty male soccer players (ages 10-16) were categorized into pre-peak height velocity (PHV) and circa-PHV groups based on maturity offset values estimated using the Mirwald equation. Sprinting speed was assessed using a 30-m sprint test. A linear mixed model analysis revealed significant improvements in sprint performance over time (p < 0.002, d = 0.78), with the circa-PHV group consistently outperforming the pre-PHV group (p < 0.001, d = 0.43). There was no significant time × maturity interaction (p = 0.722), indicating that the rate of change in sprint performance over the 12-month interval did not differ between pre- and circa-PHV players. These findings support the critical role of biological maturity in sprint progression, as more mature athletes demonstrated faster 30-m sprint performance. However, this study does not support the notion that sprinting develops at a significantly higher rate during circa-PHV than during pre-PHV.

title: Quadriceps Strength Recovery Trajectories Associate with Pre-Operative Predictors but not Clinical Outcomes Following ACL Reconstruction.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Quadriceps weakness following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) is common, however distinct longitudinal strength trajectories not have been examined. This study aimed to i) identify strength trajectories measured pre-operatively to 12 months post-ACLR, and determine associations with ii) pre-operative demographics, patient-reported outcomes (PROs: Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score [KOOS], Tegner, Marx) and ACLR concomitant surgeries, and iii) clinical outcomes post-ACLR including cartilage compositional changes (via magnetic resonance imaging [MRI] T1ρ relaxation times) and 12-month KOOS.
METHODS: Isometric quadriceps strength was measured bilaterally pre-operatively and at 4, 6, and 12 months. Group trajectory modeling characterized longitudinal strength recovery in ACLR and uninvolved limbs, which were combined to define dual-limb recovery patterns. Tibiofemoral and patellofemoral cartilage composition was measured pre-operatively and at 12 months post-ACLR. Dirichlet regressions examined associations between trajectories and demographics, surgeries, PROs, and cartilage changes.
RESULTS: 59 participants were included (58% female; age, 21.9 ± 4.7y; BMI, 24.55 ± 3.7kg/m 2). Three combined trajectories were identified: bilaterally weak (51%), which demonstrated uninvolved limb strength declines and failure to recover ACLR limb pre-operative strength; bilaterally strong (38%), which demonstrated minimal uninvolved limb declines and ACLR limb pre-operative strength recovery; and weak uninvolved, strong ACLR limb (12%). Lower pre-injury Tegner scores associated with bilaterally weak membership (p = 0.01), where probability increased from 0.27 (score of 10) to 0.61 (score of 0). Medial meniscectomy associated most with bilaterally weak membership (p<.001, 0.86 probability). No associations were found between trajectories and clinical outcomes.
CONCLUSIONS: While individuals who failed to restore ACLR limb strength demonstrated bilateral quadriceps weakness pre-operatively, persons who demonstrated greater pre-operative bilateral strength recovered ACLR limb strength. Medial meniscectomy associated with an inability to restore quadriceps strength.

title: Work-related musculoskeletal pain, fatigue, and dietary habits in athletic trainers and physical therapists providing sports team support.
abstract: BackgroundAthletic professionals (athletic trainers and physical therapists) perform injury prevention, health management, evaluation, emergency care, post-injury protection, rehabilitation, and administrative duties. Their focus on athletes' health may lead them to overlook high physical and psychosocial demands that may increase musculoskeletal pain (MSP), fatigue, and unhealthy dietary habits.ObjectiveTo examine MSP, fatigue, and dietary habits among athletic professionals who provide on-site team support and explore how fatigue and dietary habits relate to MSP.MethodsParticipants were required to be athletic professionals providing on-site team support. This cross-sectional online survey assessed 3-month work-related MSP in body regions, fatigue using a modified Fatigue Assessment Scale, and dietary habits using a structured food-frequency questionnaire. Logistic regression and mediation analyses examined associations and indirect associations, adjusting for relevant confounders.ResultsA total of 132 valid responses were included. MSP was highly prevalent, particularly in the lower back (83%), wrists/fingers (80%), and neck (67%). Fatigue (OR = 3.1, 95% CI = 1.34-7.45) and several suboptimal dietary habits (e.g., irregular meal timing, inadequate intake, fast eating, unbalanced diet, replacing meals with snacks, emotional eating) were significantly associated with MSP. Exploratory mediation analyses indicated statistically significant indirect associations via inadequate intake, replacing meals with snacks, and emotional eating, suggesting these behaviours may partially account for the fatigue-MSP association.ConclusionsAthletic professionals experience a high burden of MSP, fatigue, and suboptimal dietary habits that may be interrelated in ways that exacerbate work-related health. Workplace strategies should address workload, fatigue management, and access to healthy eating options to support sustainable practice and well-being.

title: No clear association between time to return-to-play and first additional injury in European professional football players after ACL injury: A media-based study.
abstract:
PURPOSE: The primary aim of this media-based study was to investigate whether time from anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury to return to play (RTP) was associated with the hazard of a first additional injury over calendar time among male professional football players in the five major European leagues. Secondary aims were to examine associations with a first additional injury within 365 days after RTP and with the number of official competitive matches missed because of the first additional injury.
METHODS: Male professional football players who sustained an ACL injury, underwent ACL reconstruction and returned to official competition were identified from publicly available data. RTP was defined as the first official competitive match after ACL injury. Cox proportional hazards regression assessed associations over the full follow-up and within 365 days, adjusted for age and player position. Sensitivity analysis examined predefined RTP categories; negative binomial regression assessed the association between time to RTP and the number of official competitive matches missed because of the first additional injury.
RESULTS: Among 278 players, mean time to RTP was 242.3 ± 99.5 days and 201 (72.3%) sustained a first additional injury. No clear evidence of an association was observed between time to RTP and the hazard of a first additional injury over the full follow-up or within 365 days. Similarly, no clear evidence of an association was observed in the categorical sensitivity analysis or between time to RTP and the number of matches missed because of the first additional injury.
CONCLUSIONS: No clear evidence of an association was observed between time from ACL injury to RTP and the hazard of a first additional injury either over the full follow-up period or within 365 days after RTP. Similarly, no clear evidence of an association was observed between time to RTP and the number of official competitive matches missed because of the first additional injury.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV.

title: Hitting Volume Demands during Men's Australian Open and Roland Garros: Effects of Tournament, Competition Phase, and Player Level.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hitting volume is a key component of external load in tennis, as it reflects the cumulative demands associated with the repetitive execution of complex stroke actions during match play. Despite its relevance for workload monitoring and injury prevention, limited information is available regarding how hitting volume demands vary according to playing surface, tournament progression, and player level in elite professional tennis.
HYPOTHESIS: Hitting volume demands vary according to tournament, competition phase, and player ranking level.
STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional observational study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: Match data were collected from 474 player-match observations (236 at the Australian Open and 238 at Roland Garros). Complete stroke count data were available for 384 player-match observations, comprising 214,874 analyzed strokes. Match duration, stroke counts, and rally length distributions were compared across tournaments, competition phases, and ranking groups.
RESULTS: Roland Garros matches were characterized by greater overall hitting volumes than Australian Open matches (P = 0.04), despite a similar number of points played. These differences were reflected in higher groundstroke volumes and a greater proportion of medium and long rallies at Roland Garro (P < 0.05). Competition phase was associated with differences in selected stroke-count variables and rally structure, with later-round matches showing a greater proportion of prolonged rallies (P < 0.05), although overall match duration and total stroke volume remained comparable. Differences according to player level were also identified. Top 10 players accumulated lower overall hitting volumes (P < 0.05) and exhibited a lower proportion of short rallies together with a greater proportion of prolonged exchanges than lower-ranked players (P < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: Hitting volume demands were associated with tournament, competition phase, and player ranking level. These contextual factors should be considered when interpreting competition loads and planning training and recovery strategies during Grand Slam competition.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The reported competition reference values may assist coaches and sports medicine practitioners in optimizing surface-specific training prescription, workload monitoring, fatigue management, and return-to-play strategies in professional tennis.

title: Research trends in total knee arthroplasty in India: a five-year bibliometric analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Total Knee Arthroplasty (TKA) is one of the fastest-growing orthopaedic procedures in India, driven by demographic transitions, increased life expectancy, and the rising burden of knee osteoarthritis. With expanding procedural volumes, periodic evaluation of scientific output is essential to identify evolving research priorities, institutional leadership, and collaborative patterns. This study aimed to perform a bibliometric analysis of Indian TKA research published over the past five years.
METHODS: Publications were retrieved from the Scopus database using a structured search strategy for TKA-related terms. The search was restricted to studies published between 1 January 2021 and 30 December 2025 and conducted in an Indian setting. Bibliometric indicators assessed publication trends, document types, journals, authorship, institutional productivity, and state-wise contributions. Network-based bibliometric visualizations were generated using VOSviewer.
RESULTS: A total of 860 publications were identified, showing a steady increase in research output with peak productivity in 2025 (n = 221). Maharashtra and Delhi were the leading contributors, and the All-India Institute of Medical Sciences was the most productive institution. Original research articles accounted for 69.5% of publications. Emerging themes included robotic-assisted surgery, AI-based modeling, and advanced rehabilitation. International collaboration was observed in 24.18% of studies, mainly with the UK and USA.
CONCLUSION: Indian TKA research has demonstrated substantial growth and increasing thematic maturity over the past five years, with a shift toward technology-driven and collaborative research. Strengthening national registries, encouraging multicentric collaboration, and expanding research beyond metropolitan centers are essential to sustain future impact.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Not applicable.

title: Body Image, Disordered Eating, and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport Risk in Female Athletes: Associations Across Psychological and Behavioral Factors.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs) is traditionally conceptualized as a physiological consequence of low energy availability, yet emerging evidence implicates psychological and behavioral mechanisms in its development. This study examined the associations among body image, disordered eating, social physique anxiety, and female health knowledge to clarify psychosocial antecedents of REDs risk in female athletes.
HYPOTHESIS: Negative body image will be associated with REDs risk and disordered eating.
STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 4.
METHODS: A total of 105 female athletes (mean age, 21.7 ± 3.4 years) completed validated measures assessing body image, social physique anxiety, disordered eating, REDs risk, and female health knowledge. Pearson correlations, multiple regression, and mediation analyses were performed to examine psychological predictors and mediating pathways of REDs risk.
RESULTS: Negative body image was associated strongly with REDs risk (r = 0.61; P < 0.001) and remained the dominant independent correlate (β = 0.48; P < 0.001). Disordered eating was identified as a significant statistical mediator of the association between negative body image and REDs risk (indirect = 1.17; 95% CI, 0.46, 1.86), while the direct effect persisted (c' = 1.89; 95% CI, 0.91, 2.87; P < 0.001). Positive body image exerted a protective influence (β = -1.47; P < 0.001), and social physique anxiety showed a small, nonsignificant, association (β = 0.18; P = 0.05). Female health knowledge demonstrated a significant inverse bivariate association with REDs risk (r = -0.28; P = 0.002), although this relationship was not retained in multivariable analyses. The model explained 44% of variance (R ² = 0.44; P < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: Findings support an association between body image disturbance, disordered eating behaviors, and REDs risk in female athletes. Positive body image and female health knowledge may serve protective roles. Integrating psychological screening and assets-based education into REDs prevention could shift practice from reactive physiological detection toward proactive, holistic athlete healthcare.

title: The Use of Cupping (Hijama) Therapy Among Athletes and Its Relationship With Sleep Quality: A Cross-Sectional Study in Palestine.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Wet cupping, or Hijama, is commonly used by athletes for recovery, yet evidence regarding its relationship with sleep quality remains limited. This study examined cupping use, perceived benefits, adverse effects, and factors associated with self-reported sleep quality among Palestinian athletes.
METHODS: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among Palestinian athletes. Of 754 athletes screened at nine sports clubs and training centers across the West Bank, 470 (62.3%) reported previous wet-cupping use; 468 had sufficient primary-outcome data and were analyzed. Data were collected using a structured paper-based questionnaire incorporating the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. Analyses included descriptive statistics, exact and chi-square tests, Spearman correlations, multiple linear regression, and path analysis.
RESULTS: Improved mobility (30.8%), reduced muscle cramps (25.6%), enhanced immunity (16.2%), and increased endurance (9.0%) were the most frequently reported intended benefits. Cupping was commonly reported for chronic or recurrent conditions (99.6%), muscle strain (41.5%), and headaches (41.2%). Higher BMI and greater cupping-session frequency were associated with greater perceived cupping benefit (p = 0.010 and p < 0.001, respectively). Reported inflammation was associated with BMI category, gender, and competition level, while mild pain was associated with BMI category and competition level. Lower PSQI scores were associated with higher BMI, greater cupping-session frequency, and greater perceived cupping benefit. In the multivariable model, higher BMI, vitamin use, greater cupping-session frequency, greater perceived benefit, and manual rather than automated suction were independently associated with lower PSQI scores. The model explained 35.2% of the variance in sleep quality.
CONCLUSION: Cupping-related practices and participant characteristics were associated with sleep quality. More frequent sessions, vitamin use, manual suction, higher BMI, and greater perceived benefit were associated with better sleep quality. These findings do not establish causality. Prospective studies are needed before cupping can be recommended to improve sleep or recovery.

title: Unsupervised Machine Learning Identifies Shared Biomechanical and Clinical Variation in Individuals with Knee Osteoarthritis and High BMI: A Secondary Analysis of the IDEA Trial.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: High body mass index (BMI≥27 kg/m2) and aberrant gait biomechanics are primary risk factors for knee osteoarthritis (KOA), yet the specific loading patterns linked to clinical disease features remain unclear. Unsupervised machine learning (ML) was used to identify vertical ground reaction force (vGRF) waveform modes of variation and characterize the shared and individual variation between vGRF profiles and clinical features in individuals with KOA and high BMI.
METHODS: Baseline gait and clinical data from the Intensive Diet and Exercise for Arthritis (IDEA) trial (n=431; 29% male; 65±6 years; 34±4 kg/m2) were analyzed. vGRF waveforms (n=2,394) were represented using three functional data analysis methods: time- and bodyweight-normalization; elastic shape analysis; and optimal transport (OT). Principal component analysis extracted the dominant vGRF modes of variation, and Data Integration Via Analysis of Subspaces (DIVAS) quantified shared and individual variation among vGRF profiles and 40 clinical features.
RESULTS: A sustained loading phenotype emerged across all vGRF representations (lesser early and late stance vGRF; greater midstance vGRF). DIVAS identified shared variation between sustained loading and higher BMI, elevated inflammatory biomarkers, greater pain, worse KL grade, and slower walking speed. OT identified a temporal loading phenotype that shared variation with female sex.
CONCLUSIONS: Unsupervised ML identified a sustained loading biomechanical phenotype that shared variation with greater BMI, increased inflammation, worse radiographic severity, and slower walking speed. These data highlight the complex interplay among gait biomechanics and clinical KOA features in individuals with high BMI and may help to guide future work evaluating targeted gait retraining interventions.

title: From Sudden Cardiac Death Prevention to Performance Optimization: A Conceptual Framework for Cardiovascular Assessment in Elite Athletes.
abstract: Cardiovascular pre-participation evaluation in elite athletes primarily aims to identify cardiovascular conditions associated with sudden cardiac death. Current international recommendations emphasize comprehensive medical history, physical examination, and resting 12-lead electrocardiography (ECG), with additional investigations guided by clini-cal findings and individual risk. However, advances in sports cardiology, cardiovascular imaging, and exercise physiology provide opportunities to integrate cardiovascular risk assessment with physiological performance evaluation. This article proposes a concep-tual, hypothesis-generating framework integrating structural, electrical, and functional cardiovascular assessment in elite athletes. The framework consists of 3 sequential components: comprehensive clinical assessment with resting ECG; transthoracic echo-cardiography for structural evaluation and longitudinal reference; and cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) as an optional complementary investigation. Cardiopulmonary exercise testing may provide information on maximal oxygen uptake, ventilatory thresh-olds, oxygen pulse, ventilatory efficiency, heart rate recovery, and exercise-induced arrhythmias, potentially supporting individualized training prescription and longitudinal physiological monitoring. Cardiac magnetic resonance and coronary computed tomog-raphy angiography (CCTA) may be considered selectively when clinically indicated. A one-time CCTA strategy during an athlete's career is proposed as a research hypothesis requiring prospective assessment of clinical utility and cost-effectiveness. Importantly, CPET and CCTA are not proposed as universal screening requirements. This framework is intended to complement, rather than replace, current evidence-based international recommendations. As the proposed model is based on available literature and expert opinion and has not undergone prospective clinical validation, future multicenter stud-ies are required to determine whether integrated cardiovascular assessment improves risk stratification, athlete safety, clinical decision-making, performance monitoring, and cost-effectiveness.

title: Endocrine dynamics of special operations forces across mission cycles: implications for human stress physiology.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This study investigates the endocrine responses and muscle damage markers in elite male Special Operations Force operators across operational phases to understand hormonal adaptations to extreme operational stress and recovery.
METHODS: Fifty-six operators (28-42 years) participated in a longitudinal study conducted at a Special Operations Forces unit. Blood samples were collected at three visits: Visit 1 (baseline recovery), Visit 2 (intensive pre-deployment training), and Visit 3 (post-deployment recovery). Serum concentrations of testosterone (T), cortisol (CORT), dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEA-S), growth hormone (GH), insulin-like growth factor-I (IGF-I), progesterone (P4), creatine kinase (CK), and myoglobin (Mb) were analyzed.
RESULTS: Post-deployment (Visit 3), T levels increased (+ 20%, p < 0.05), and CORT decreased (- 23%, p < 0.05), resulting in a significantly higher testosterone-to-cortisol ratio compared with Visit 1 and Visit 2 (p ≤ 0.05). DHEA-S correlated with CORT (r = 0.37, p < 0.05), suggesting a compensatory adrenal response under stress. GH concentrations were markedly reduced post-deployment (- 84%, p ≤ 0.05), while IGF-I remained stable, indicating differential regulation within the GH-IGF-I axis during recovery. P4 concentrations remained elevated across all phases, reflecting a consistent endocrine feature across operational phases rather than a defined mechanistic adaptation. No significant changes were observed in CK or Mb, underscoring effective physical stress management at the time of post-deployment sampling.
CONCLUSION: These findings emphasize the importance of tailored training and recovery strategies for sustaining endocrine balance, resilience, and operational readiness in elite military personnel.

title: Ergogenic effects of beetroot juice supplementation on neuromuscular function and simulated combat demands in elite female taekwondo athletes.
abstract: Beetroot juice supplementation has been widely examined across various sport disciplines due to its potential ergogenic effects. However, evidence regarding its impact on combat sports particularly in female athletes remains limited. The aim of this study was to evaluate the acute effects of beetroot juice supplementation on simulated taekwondo combat performance and neuromuscular function in elite female taekwondo athletes. Seven elite female Olympic taekwondo athletes (age: 20.3 ± 3.7 years), participated in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study consisting of two experimental trials). Each trial involved the consumption of either 140 mL of beetroot juice (which contains 12.8 mmol NO₃⁻) or 140 mL of a placebo (with 0.08 mmol NO₃⁻) followed by a simulated taekwondo combat session and assessments of neuro-muscular function (i.e., vertical jump and visual cognitive performance). In addition, metabolic (i.e., blood lactate), and perceptual responses (i.e., rate of perceived exertion) were measured before, after, and 3 minutes post-combat. No significant differences during the simulated taekwondo combat (e.g., attack time; p = 0.531-0.989; ηp² = 0.01-0.05), neuromuscular function battery (p = 0.302-0.700; ηp² = 0.02-0.04), blood lactate concentrations (p = 0.705; ηp² = 0.13), or rate of perceived exertion values (RPE) (p = 0.717; ηp² = 0.12) were obtained between beetroot juice and placebo conditions. Acute ingestion of beetroot juice (140 mL) did not enhance simulated combat performance or neuromuscular function in female Olympic taekwondo athletes.

title: Physical examination of the cervical spine should be conducted in female athletes with a history of concussion.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Female athletes may be at increased risk of injury following sports-related concussion (SRC), even after symptom resolution. Residual cervical spine impairments have been proposed as a potential contributor; however, these have not been well characterised in female athletes. This study aimed to examine whether a history of SRC was associated with clinical assessments of the cervical spine in female athletes.
METHODS: In this cross-sectional observational study, 156 elite and pre-elite female athletes from water polo, soccer, diving, rugby-7s and cycling/BMX were recruited. History of SRC within the previous 12 months was self-reported. Assessments included questionnaires and physical examination of the cervical spine, comprising range of motion, manual examination, joint position error (JPE) and maximal isometric neck strength. Between-group differences were examined using univariable statistical analyses.
RESULTS: Athletes with a history of SRC demonstrated a higher prevalence of reduced cervical range of motion, positive findings on manual examination, increased JPE and a history of headaches or migraines compared with athletes without concussion history. No deficits in maximal isometric neck strength were observed in athletes with a history of SRC.
CONCLUSION: Cervical spine impairments were more commonly observed in female athletes with a history of SRC within the previous 12 months, including in athletes who did not report current neck pain. These findings suggest consideration of targeted cervical spine assessment beyond symptom-based screening in athletes with a concussion history. Whether identification and management of cervical spine impairments influence subsequent injury risk requires investigation in prospective and interventional studies.

title: Low Physical Therapy Referral Rates for Knee Osteoarthritis Present a Barrier to Care for Patients With Medicaid.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the rates of physical therapy (PT) referral for knee osteoarthritis (KOA) and factors associated with referral patterns, including insurance status, provider specialty, year, and patient demographics and comorbidities.
DESIGN: This retrospective cohort study included 41,373 patients diagnosed with KOA at an integrated health system in Arizona and Colorado, USA between January 2020 and February 2023. PT referral rates were stratified by insurance type. Multivariable logistic regression assessed predictors of referral including insurance type, age, BMI, sex, race/ethnicity, provider specialty, year of visit, and comorbidities.
RESULTS: Crude PT referral rates at the initial visit were 12.06% for Medicaid, 6.83% for Medicare, 10.29% for commercial insurance, and 8.33% for uninsured patients. Adjusted analysis showed that Medicaid patients had higher referral odds (OR, 1.20; 95% CI [1.10, 1.30]; p < 0.001), whereas Medicare patients had lower odds (OR, 0.76; 95% CI [0.66, 0.88]; p < 0.001) compared to those with commercial insurance. Female (OR, 1.21; 95% CI [1.14, 1.29]; p < 0.001) and Hispanic patients (OR 1.18; 95% CI [1.09, 1.29]; p < 0.001) demonstrated increased referral odds. Provider specialty was associated with PT referral, with non-operative sports medicine providers having the highest referral odds (OR, 3.00; 95% CI [2.72, 3.31]; p < 0.001) relative to orthopaedic surgery.
CONCLUSION: Despite strong clinical practice guidelines recommending PT, formal referral rates for patients with KOA remain low regardless of insurance type, patient characteristics, and referring healthcare provider specialty. Low formal PT referral rates may represent a barrier to evidence-based KOA care.

title: Integrated physical, cognitive and psychological rehabilitation following multiple ACL reconstructions in a professional handball player: a case report.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries with repeated surgical interventions and postoperative complications pose a major challenge in sports rehabilitation. Beyond neuromuscular deficits, psychological and cognitive readiness often remain impaired, increasing reinjury risk and threatening athletic careers. This case highlights an integrated rehabilitation strategy addressing physical, psychological, and cognitive domains in a professional athlete with a complex surgical history.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 31-year-old white Serbian male professional handball player with a history of two ACL reconstructions, meniscal repairs, a postoperative knee infection, and multiple arthroscopic interventions presented with persistent knee instability, pain, and psychological distress. Following repeated failed return-to-play attempts, he underwent a ten-week intervention combining therapeutic exercises, sports psychology sessions, and neurocognitive dual-task training. Pre- and post-intervention assessments included gait analysis, postural control, strength testing, ACL-specific functional tests, and psychological evaluations. Post-intervention assessments showed improvements in gait mechanics, postural stability, neuromuscular strength, and reduced functional asymmetries, alongside lower cognitive anxiety and greater motivation.
CONCLUSIONS: This case suggests that an interdisciplinary, multimodal rehabilitation approach, integrating physical, psychological, and cognitive strategies, may help address both physical deficits and psychological barriers in athletes with multiple ACL surgeries and complex postoperative courses. Such integration may support function, confidence, and readiness in high-performance athletes facing career-threatening injuries.

title: Persistent and recurrent musculoskeletal pain in young athletes: an overlooked biopsychosocial determinant of return to sport trajectories - a focused narrative review.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Persistent and recurrent musculoskeletal pain is common in young athletes, yet its role in recovery and return to sport (RTS) decision-making remains insufficiently acknowledged. In youth sport, pain is often normalized or viewed primarily through an injury-centered lens, despite its potential to shape function, participation patterns, and athletic trajectories over time.
AREAS COVERED: This focused narrative review aimed to (1) synthesize current evidence on persistent and recurrent musculoskeletal pain in young athletes and (2) propose a developmentally informed biopsychosocial framework for understanding its implications for RTS. Electronic searches were conducted in PubMed, PsycINFO, and SPORTDiscus for studies published from 1 January 2006, through 28 February 2026, supplemented by backward and forward citation tracking and targeted hand-searching of reference lists. It integrates evidence on definitions, prevalence, clinical presentation, psychosocial and contextual factors, functional interference, and RTS decision-making, conceptualizing ongoing pain as an overlooked determinant of RTS trajectories.
EXPERT OPINION/COMMENTARY: In young athletes, pain should not be treated as a peripheral symptom or addressed only when recovery is delayed. More informed RTS decisions require attention not only to physical recovery markers, but also to how pain is experienced, interpreted, and managed throughout recovery. A developmentally informed biopsychosocial perspective may support earlier recognition, safer return decisions, more stable participation, and better long-term health outcomes.

title: Spaceflight human optimization and performance: positioning astronauts in an operational framework to promote health, fitness, and mission readiness.
abstract: Optimizing astronaut mission readiness is a multidisciplinary endeavor that should integrate concepts from aerospace medicine, human performance, sports science, nutrition, and engineering. Situating astronauts within a theoretical framework similar to that of operational athletes, while addressing top human systems capability needs outlined for future missions, may be optimal for promoting sustained health and performance before, during, and after missions to low-Earth orbit, the lunar surface, and Mars. Mission readiness can be optimized by enhancing physiological and behavioral/psychological performance through data-driven and individualized exercise countermeasures, health and performance monitoring, precision nutrition, and rehabilitation strategies. Appropriate and stable space food systems that facilitate adequate provision of nutrients and fluids to prime astronauts for mission-critical tasks and operational demands are needed, though research is needed into potential nutritional considerations that might be useful for future missions. Behavioral readiness programs should emphasize stress inoculation, adaptive decision-making, communication, Earth-independent operation functionality, conflict resolution, leadership, and team-based problem-solving before flight to promote healthy team dynamics in-flight, along with proper society reintegration and uptake of family and occupational roles post-flight. Exercise remains an essential countermeasure during spaceflight, with an emphasis on maximizing fitness before launch to mitigate in-flight declines and on maintaining fitness levels and functionality during flight through high-intensity multimodal exercise. Following return to Earth, rehabilitative programs serve to restore cardiovascular, sensorimotor, and skeletal function, followed by enhancing skill-based performance components through a phase-based training program. Continuous monitoring systems that provide insight into health, performance, sleep, cognitive, nutritional, and recovery status should enable data-driven decision-making on physical readiness across all mission phases. By integrating insight from multiple disciplines, this unifying approach delivers a theoretical framework for sustaining astronaut health and performance during extended-duration missions.

title: Editorial Commentary: Allograft Reconstruction in Chronic Proximal Hamstring Tendon Avulsions: Bridging the Gap May Not Equal a Full Return.
abstract: Proximal hamstring tendon avulsions are being treated surgically at rising rates, and although primary repair reliably restores function and return to sport in the acute setting, chronic and significantly retracted tears present a far more difficult problem. When direct repair is not feasible for a chronic, retracted proximal hamstring tendon avulsion, allograft reconstruction offers a bridge across a gap that would otherwise go unaddressed. However, significant chronicity and retraction are difficult challenges to overcome, and patient expectations must be appropriately counseled. As a salvage procedure, allograft reconstruction may improve patient outcomes significantly; however, it is not expected to restore full function, return athletic individuals to their baseline and preinjury level of sports participation, or match the success of primary repair. Allograft reconstruction may also carry more than double the risk of rerupture, which is important to discuss with patients up front. Graft choice and postoperative rehabilitation protocols remain heterogeneous across the limited available literature, and a validated tool to risk-stratify which chronic, retracted tears are best served by reconstruction versus continued nonoperative management does not yet exist. These findings suggest that allograft reconstruction is a viable and clinically meaningful option for a difficult, often nonoperatively unsalvageable problem, but surgeons should frame it for patients as a salvage procedure rather than a full restoration of function, and expectations should be set accordingly.

title: Ultrasound-guided injection treatments for tendinopathy: an update.
abstract: The choice of treatment for chronic tendinopathy and related peritendinous conditions has become challenging as multiple options are available. When conservative treatments fail, injections of platelet-rich plasma (PRP), corticosteroids, and hyaluronic acid have become important in the management of these conditions. Other interventions, such as dry-needling, percutaneous tenotomy, percutaneous release, and hydrodissection, may also be used. Ultrasound guidance allows real-time visualization of the needle relative to its target and adjacent neurovascular structures. This is particularly advantageous for deep or small-caliber tendons, for procedures requiring precise intratendinous or peritendinous needle placement (e.g., PRP injection, hydrodissection), and for percutaneous release, where a blind approach carries a materially higher risk of neurovascular or tendon injury. This review summarizes the mechanism of action, technique, evidence, and indications for the injection treatments currently used for tendinopathy, and outlines the general principles of ultrasound-guided injection technique.

title: Field-Based Assessment of Running Biomechanics Using Global Positioning System/Inertial Measurement Unit: Establishing Construct Validity in Elite Athletes.
abstract: Weber, JA, Peeling, P, Hart, NH, and Newton, RU. Field-based assessment of running biomechanics using global positioning system/inertial measurement unit: Establishing construct validity in elite athletes. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-To examine the between-session reliability and construct validity of global positioning system (GPS)/inertial measurement unit (IMU)-derived biomechanical variables during field-based running in elite athletes. Fifty-four professional male Australian Football League players completed repeated 40-m runs across 1 competitive season (3,943 trials). Running speed for the 20-40 m segment was quantified via 10-Hz GPS and center-of-mass displacement metrics derived from a 100-Hz IMU. Between-session reliability (n = 25, mean (k) = 2.95) was assessed using a linear mixed-effects model with velocity as a fixed covariate, expressed as intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) (absolute agreement), SEM, and minimal detectable change95, with 95% confidence intervals from athlete-cluster bootstrap. Five candidate models were compared; Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines was selected based on lowest cross-validation root mean squared error (RMSE). Validity was assessed over 100 iterations of athlete-stratified cross-validation (80/20 split), with agreement quantified by ICC, RMSE, and athlete-level Bland-Altman analysis. Velocity-adjusted reliability ranged from moderate to good-to-excellent across 12 variables (ICC = 0.65-0.92), with 8 meeting good-to-excellent thresholds (ICC ≥0.75). Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines accounted for 93% of variance in running speed (R2 = 0.93; RMSE = 0.20 m·s-1; ICC = 0.96 ± 0.004). Athlete-level Bland-Altman analysis indicated negligible bias (-0.01 m·s-1; LoA: -0.243 to +0.223 m·s-1) with no proportional bias (p = 0.369); limits narrowed in athletes with adequate data volume (n = 47; -0.207 to +0.189 m·s-1). Mechanics-speed relationships persisted after accounting for within-athlete clustering (residual between-athlete ICC = 0.43), and the most influential predictors were consistent with established biomechanical determinants of speed. These findings support GPS/IMU-derived biomechanical variables as field-based indicators of running mechanics. Pending replication and criterion validation, this approach may offer practitioners an accessible framework for monitoring performance and rehabilitation.

title: ATG5-overexpressing MSCs improve ligament healing with an associated shift toward M2 macrophage polarization in aged rats.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Autophagy is crucial for maintaining mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) function, yet its role in age-related ligament healing deficits remains unclear. This study examined the relationship between MSC autophagic activity and age-related ligament healing and evaluated ATG5 overexpression effects on autophagy and regeneration.
METHODS: Medial collateral ligament (MCL) injury models were established in young and aged rats. Healing was assessed using ultrasound, histology, immunohistochemistry, apoptosis assays, and biomechanical testing. Aged MSCs were engineered to overexpress ATG5 and transplanted into injured ligaments. Repair outcomes and macrophage polarization changes were evaluated.
RESULTS: Aged rats exhibited impaired ligament healing, and aged MSCs displayed reduced autophagic activity. ATG5 overexpression enhanced autophagy in aged MSCs, and transplantation of ATG5-overexpressing MSCs was associated with improved ligament repair in aged rats, including increased proliferation, angiogenesis, collagen organization, and biomechanical strength, alongside reduced apoptosis. ATG5-overexpressing MSC transplantation was also associated with lower M1 and higher M2 macrophage markers and a more anti-inflammatory cytokine profile. Reduced MSC autophagy was associated with age-related ligament healing deficits.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings support a potential relationship among ATG5-associated autophagy, macrophage phenotype, and improved ligament repair, while the causal dependence of therapeutic effects on autophagy and macrophage polarization remains to be established.

title: More than fuel: Why athletes need better language around food.
abstract: "Food is fuel" is a widely used phrase in sport settings intended to emphasize the importance of nutrition for performance. While nutrition is essential for health and success, this framing may unintentionally reinforce a narrow, performance-oriented understanding of eating that has implications for athletes' relationships with food and their bodies. Athletes are at heightened risk for eating concerns, low energy availability, and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs), and aspects of sport culture may contribute to rigid, rule-based approaches to eating. This commentary argues that "food is fuel" language reflects and reinforced broader sports norms centered around optimization, control, and performance. Potential consequences include reduced attunement to internal cues and the moralization of food choices, particularly in sport environments where appearance and performance are closely intertwined. Language is proposed as a modifiable factor for prevention and more flexible, athlete-centered approaches to discussing food and eating are identified. Rather than dismissing the importance of nutrition in athletics, this commentary advocates for broader conceptualizations of eating that acknowledge its physical, psychological, social, and cultural functions and support athletes in developing sustainable relationships with food throughout and beyond their athletic careers.

title: Imaging of acute sports injuries of the shoulder girdle.
abstract: Acute injuries of the shoulder girdle commonly result from sports activities and lead to imaging studies. Radiologists who interpret these studies should be familiar with traumatic mechanisms and the imaging manifestations of glenohumeral dislocation, acromioclavicular sprain, rotator cuff tear, labral tear, osseous contusion or fracture, and myotendinous strain. Imaging findings are crucial for making accurate diagnoses, grading the severity of injuries, guiding treatment plans, and managing the athletes' expectations for rehabilitation and return to sport. In this review article, we address common and uncommon injuries in both young and mature athletes. Focusing on magnetic resonance imaging, we provide examples of classic injuries and discuss pitfalls that challenge diagnostic interpretation.

title: Advanced Footwear Technology in Distance Running: What We Know, What We Don't Know, and Future Directions.
abstract: Over the past decade, running shoes have undergone substantial innovation with the emergence of Advanced Footwear Technology (AFT). Shoes with AFT are typically characterized by highly compliant (deformable) and resilient (high energy return) midsole foams, embedded curved stiffening elements, low mass, and a rockered longitudinal geometry. This expert statement aims to synthesize established knowledge, remaining uncertainties and key directions for future research on AFT in middle- and long-distance running. Current literature demonstrates robust improvements in running economy and performance with AFT, with reported metabolic savings of approximately 2%-4%, and corresponding performance improvements of 1%-3%. These benefits likely arise from a combination of "acute" and possibly "long-term" mechanisms. Proposed acute mechanisms include decreased muscle force production due to higher positive work from energy-returning foams, lower muscle force production to accommodate mechanical running demands due to compliant midsoles, and improved mechanical efficiency associated with greater longitudinal bending stiffness and curved geometry. Importantly, AFT features have a synergistic effect, with the relative importance of each mechanism differing depending on the context. Emerging evidence also suggests potential reductions in muscle damage/inflammation and soreness, which could support better physiological resilience, and higher training volumes/quality. From a biomechanical injury risk perspective, AFT can redistribute loading, potentially increasing metatarsal and tarsal stress while reducing tibia and possibly Achilles tendon loading. However, injury risk associated with AFT use remains equivocal, with limited high-quality data. Notably, substantial inter-individual variability has been observed, influencing both running economy and potential injury risk although the determinants of this variability remain unclear.

title: Wearable Technologies and Artificial Intelligence in Sports Medicine: A Systematic Narrative Review of Injury Prevention and Rehabilitation.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Wearable technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) are shifting sports medicine from episodic, subjective assessment toward continuous, data-driven injury surveillance. This review aimed to map the main wearable sensor modalities used in injury prevention and rehabilitation, evaluate AI architectures applied to biomechanical and physiological data, summarize clinically relevant applications by anatomical region, and identify methodological, ethical, and implementation challenges.
METHODS: A systematic narrative review was conducted across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for studies published from 2016 to 2026, supplemented by manual reference screening. Search terms combined wearable sensors, AI and machine learning, and sports medicine outcomes. After title and abstract screening of 614 records and full-text assessment of 87 articles, 28 studies met the inclusion criteria.
RESULTS: Inertial measurement units, GPS/GNSS, surface electromyography, and photoplethysmography were the most frequently reported sensor modalities. Deep learning, ensemble methods, and multimodal fusion were commonly used to process biomechanical and physiological signals. One hybrid IMU-sEMG study involving 50 athletes reported 92.3% accuracy, 90.5% recall, and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.93 for classifying biomechanical injury-risk states. An ankle-monitoring study using data from 87 athletes across 12 sports reported 87.4% overall detection accuracy, a 12.1% false-alarm rate, and 17.2 ms latency. However, substantial heterogeneity in study design, populations, outcomes, and validation methods prevented direct comparison or pooled quantitative interpretation.
CONCLUSION: Wearable-AI systems show promising potential for injury-risk monitoring, rehabilitation, and return-to-play support. Wider clinical adoption will require more diverse populations, longitudinal and field-based validation, improved model interpretability, standardized protocols, and robust ethical, legal, and governance frameworks.
