title: From young aces to injury cases: a qualitative study of stakeholder perspectives on injury risk in junior to elite badminton.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Competitive badminton is associated with a considerable burden of injuries, particularly during the transition from junior to elite level (ages 16-20). While the sport's dynamic stroke and movement patterns may contribute to injury risk, the factors stakeholders use to assess injury vulnerability remain poorly understood. However, identifying specific causes and indicators that point to an increased risk of injury is essential for prevention. Given the limited case numbers, combining data driven approaches with stakeholders' experiential knowledge may enhance risk assessment. This study explores expert judgement and heuristics regarding injury risk assessment as well as options for risk mitigation during the transitional phase.
METHODS: Twenty semi-structured in-person interviews were conducted with national-level stakeholders (9 coaches, 5 athletes, 2 association doctors, 2 physiotherapists, 2 strength and conditioning coaches) between October 2023 and July 2024. The interviews had an average duration of 54.4 min. Thematic analysis helped identify common patterns across assessments.
RESULTS: Four higher-order themes were identified: Excessive pressure, recovery deficits, unprofessional attitude, and disruptions in training continuity. Six cue families were perceived by stakeholders as informing injury risk assessment: signs of over-motivation, unprofessional attitude, the coaches' subjective perception ('coaches' eye'), upheavals in private life, exposure and signs of wear. While overlaps with the literature were found, stakeholders often downplayed commonly cited objective factors like injury history. Many cues were based on intuitive, experience-driven judgments and were therefore difficult to standardize or quantify.
CONCLUSIONS: Experts relied on relative risk judgments shaped by experience and situational impressions rather than absolute probabilities. Integrating these practitioner-derived qualitative cues with objective data may enhance context-sensitive injury risk assessment during the junior-to-elite transition. By making experiential heuristics more transparent, the findings offer a foundation for developing more targeted injury mitigation strategies in this critical developmental phase. Further empirical validation is required.

title: Evolving Management Strategies for Osteochondral Lesions of the Talus: A Contemporary Treatment Algorithm.
abstract: ➢ Osteochondral lesions of the talus (OLT) are common injuries that remain difficult to treat because of the challenge of restoring durable hyaline cartilage. Surgical outcomes are influenced by lesion size and morphology, cartilage integrity, subchondral bone involvement, and ankle stability, all of which should be considered when evaluating operative strategies.➢ Fragment fixation preserves the native osteochondral unit in lesions with a viable fragment and is primarily indicated in acute OLT. Lift-drill-fill-fix is utilized in selected chronic lesions with a salvageable fragment and compromised subchondral bone, allowing restoration of the lesion bed and stable fixation.➢ Bone marrow stimulation techniques, including microfracture, antegrade drilling, and retrograde drilling, have demonstrated improvements in pain and functional outcomes in small and contained lesions, although the long-term durability of fibrocartilaginous repair tissue remains variable.➢ Replacement procedures such as autologous osteochondral transplantation and osteochondral allograft transplantation restore the osteochondral unit and have demonstrated favorable outcomes in larger or structurally complex lesions. Cell-based and matrix-assisted cartilage restoration strategies, such as autologous chondrocyte implantation, matrix-induced autologous chondrocyte implantation, and autologous matrix-induced chondrogenesis, have demonstrated improvements in clinical outcomes and cartilage repair in selected patients with OLT.➢ Emerging restorative approaches such as scaffold-based cartilage repair, osteoperiostic autografting techniques, and biologic adjuncts including concentrated bone marrow aspirate, platelet-rich plasma, and hyaluronic acid have demonstrated promising early clinical results, although current evidence remains limited.➢ Salvage procedures, including bulk allograft transplantation, metallic resurfacing, hemiarthroplasty, and arthrodesis, may be considered for extensive lesions or after failure of prior surgical management, although outcomes remain variable, with high complication and failure rates.

title: Programmable 4D printing of sustainable multifunctional photoresins with tissue-matched mechanics for interfacial tissue regeneration.
abstract: The integrative regeneration of articular cartilage and subchondral bone remains a major clinical challenge due to the difficulties of mimicking the spatial and compositional complexity of native osteochondral tissues in artificial implants. To overcome these limitations, 3D printing has enabled personalized solutions, going beyond traditional plug-shaped scaffolds that are limited to repairing small, cylindrical focal defects. In this study, we report solvent-free 4D printing of olive oil-derived fatty amide-based acrylate photoresin for osteochondral tissue engineering applications. The physicochemical properties of the printed polymers were fine-tuned using acrylic acid as a comonomer. With optimized printing conditions, the resin can be printed into high-resolution objects with each layer of ∼50-100 μm. Depending on the resin composition, the mechanical properties of the printed polymers vary between ∼200-1400 kPa with ∼210-420% strain under tensile setting, and ∼26-98 MPa at ∼80% strain under compressive setting. The mechanical properties of the printed polymers are comparable to those of various interfacial soft tissues, including ligaments, articular cartilage, and soft collagenous bone, indicating their potential for interfacial tissue engineering applications. Furthermore, the printed polymers showed near-body temperature-responsive shape memory (4D) properties with a recovery ratio of ∼99% for optimized resin composition. In addition, the printed polymers exhibited excellent bactericidal antimicrobial activity against both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, highlighting their multifunctional nature. More importantly, the printed polymers exhibited good cytocompatibility (cell viability ∼≥90% across all samples compared to control) toward adipose-derived human mesenchymal stem cells, facilitating growth factor-free osteogenic and chondrogenic differentiation, which confirms their potential for osteochondral tissue regeneration. Overall, the newly developed biobased resin offers a low-cost, sustainable alternative for 4D printing of personalized implants for osteochondral tissue regeneration.

title: Sleep-timing irregularity moderates the within-participant association between training load and next-morning heart rate variability in university sport participants: a 28-day study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Heart rate variability (HRV) describes beat-to-beat variation in cardiac intervals; the root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD) is a time-domain index of short-term cardiac vagal modulation. We examined whether nightly deviation from habitual sleep midpoint moderated the association between prior-day internal training load and next-morning natural-log-transformed RMSSD (lnRMSSD), and whether analogous interactions were present for resting heart rate, wellness strain, and countermovement-jump (CMJ) height.
METHODS: University students engaged in regular sport training completed 28 days of habitual monitoring. Internal load was session duration multiplied by session rating of perceived exertion. Wrist actigraphy and sleep diaries estimated sleep midpoint, and 5-min morning RR recordings yielded lnRMSSD. Mixed models separated within- and between-participant components and tested within-participant load (per 100 arbitrary units [AU]) × absolute midpoint deviation (per 30 min).
RESULTS: The analysis included 1,232 mornings from 54 participants (57.4% female; age 21.0 ± 1.7 years). At each participant's mean midpoint deviation, greater-than-usual load was associated with lower next-morning lnRMSSD (β = -0.0089, 95% CI -0.0127 to -0.0051; p < 0.001). At mean load, greater-than-usual midpoint deviation was also associated with lower lnRMSSD (β = -0.0156, 95% CI -0.0268 to -0.0045; p = 0.006). The interaction was negative (β = -0.0101, 95% CI -0.0153 to -0.0048; p < 0.001). Thus, the inverse within-participant association between load and lnRMSSD strengthened as sleep-timing irregularity increased. No load-by-midpoint interaction was detected for resting heart rate, wellness strain, or CMJ height after false discovery rate adjustment. The primary interaction persisted after adjustment for prior-morning lnRMSSD (β = -0.0096, 95% CI -0.0147 to -0.0046; p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: The within-participant association between training load and next-morning cardiac vagal modulation was moderated by sleep-timing irregularity. These field-based associations do not establish a sleep mechanism, causal recovery effect, or decision threshold.

title: Imaging of Pediatric Hip Disorders in the Young Athlete.
abstract: Pediatric hip pain in young athletes encompasses a wide range of disorders related to skeletal immaturity and increasing athletic demands. Timely and accurate diagnosis is important, as delayed recognition may result in growth disturbances, instability, and long-term morbidity. Imaging plays a central role in differentiating clinically significant abnormalities from normal developmental variation and less consequential conditions. This review presents a pattern-based framework for evaluating pediatric hip pathology, organized into key categories based on dominant imaging patterns. Emphasis is placed on imaging findings that influence management and return-to-play decisions, including high-risk features and common pitfalls related to skeletal maturation. This approach provides a practical framework for diagnosis, risk stratification, and effective multidisciplinary communication.

title: Cannabigerol Enhances Muscle Strength and Performance in Dexamethasone-Treated Mice.
abstract: Sarcopenia is a major clinical condition associated with aging and is characterized by progressive loss of skeletal muscle mass and function. Resistance training is an effective intervention to counteract muscle atrophy; however, strategies that selectively enhance functional performance remain limited. Cannabigerol, a phytocannabinoid that is not a CB1 receptor agonist and therefore lacks psychotomimetic activity, has emerged as a potential modulator of neuromuscular function, although its role in skeletal muscle adaptation remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the effects of resistance exercise and cannabigerol, alone and in combination, in a dexamethasone-induced model of muscle atrophy in mice. Animals received dexamethasone (20 mg/kg, i.p.) for 12 days and were subsequently subjected to a 4-week ladder-based resistance exercise protocol. Cannabigerol (10 mg/kg, i.p.) was administered on training days. Resistance exercise restored muscle morphology and improved fatigue resistance. In contrast, cannabigerol acted mainly on neuromuscular performance, increasing muscle power while producing only a small increase in fiber cross-sectional area. Cannabigerol potentiated training-induced power output, increasing performance by ∼55% in the first week and up to ∼87% after 4 weeks compared to exercise alone. In addition, cannabigerol increased peak grip strength (∼10%) and lowered post-exercise blood lactate in sedentary animals (∼48%). These findings show that resistance exercise and cannabigerol exert complementary effects on skeletal muscleexercise promoting structural recovery and cannabigerol enhancing neuromuscular performance and lowering post-exercise lactateand support further investigation of cannabigerol as an adjunct to exercise in glucocorticoid-induced muscle atrophy.

title: Long-term endurance running training and testosterone daily variation in ageing men; a comparative cross-sectional study.
abstract: The aim of this study was to assess the relationship between long-term endurance running training and daily variation in testosterone, which is known to diminish during ageing, in a comparative, cross-sectional study. We recruited 45 male participants into four groups [young athletes (YA), young sedentary (YS), master athletes (MA) and elderly sedentary (ES)] and performed anthropometry, strength and ergometry tests. Morning (AM) and afternoon (PM) venous blood samples were collected to evaluate testosterone daily variation, sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG), cortisol and estradiol, and we calculated free testosterone, bioavailable testosterone and the free androgen index. Two-way and three-way ANOVAs followed by Bonferroni's multiple comparisons tests were performed. The free testosterone and free androgen index showed a significant PM decrease in the MA group (P = 0.0009 and 0.0021, respectively), comparable to YA and YS; however, in the ES group there was no difference between AM and PM values (both P > 0.9999). SHBG levels were significantly increased by both the age (P = 0.0001) and activity (P = 0.0016) factors, leading to a significant decrease in free testosterone, bioavailable testosterone and free androgen index. In the peak power output parameters of ergometry, expressed in both absolute and relative values, MA achieved values comparable to YS, significantly higher than ES (P = 0.0020 and P < 0.0001, respectively) and lower than YA (P < 0.0001). In conclusion, long-term endurance running training in elderly men might be associated with the presence of daily variation in free testosterone and higher performance levels in comparison to sedentary counterparts, but it might contribute to age-related changes in SHBG and related testosterone fraction levels.

title: Running on Empty: Relative Energy Deficiency in a Military Endurance Athlete.
abstract: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sports (RED-S) is a clinical syndrome characterized by low caloric intake relative to energy expenditure, resulting in a cascade of endocrine, metabolic, and musculoskeletal consequences. In females, hallmark features include decreased bone mineral density and menstrual dysfunction, though the syndrome affects multiple organ systems in both sexes. We present the case of a 22-year-old active-duty military member who suffered recurrent stress fractures, irregular menstrual cycles, and chronic fatigue that impacted her duty status. She was noted to have a long history of non-intentional calorie restriction and was eventually diagnosed with RED-S. Treatment consisted of a multidisciplinary approach, resulting in objective improvement in bone density and a successful return to full duty status. This case highlights the importance of early diagnosis and appropriate treatment of RED-S among military members to decrease morbidity and prevent limitations to military readiness and career progression.

title: The relationship of grip and three-point pinch strength to ball velocity and elbow varus torque in high school pitchers.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hand and forearm strength play an essential role in modulating and controlling forces across the elbow during pitching. In particular, grip and pinch strength reflect functional capacity of the flexor-pronator mass, which contributes to both performance and dynamic stability of the elbow. While diminished grip strength is often used clinically to monitor recovery following shoulder and elbow injury, values in adolescent pitchers are lacking. Furthermore, the relationship between grip and pinch strength with ball velocity and elbow varus torque remains poorly defined.
METHODS: Thirty-eight healthy high school pitchers (16.0 ± 0.9 years, 183.3 ± 6.0 cm, 78.1 ± 9.2 kg) were included in this study. Bilateral grip and three-point pinch strength were assessed prior to pitching. Pitchers were then analyzed using 3D motion capture (480 Hz) and ball velocity was recorded with Trackman throwing fastballs. The pitch with the greatest ball velocity was used in the analysis. Paired t-tests compared dominant and non-dominant grip and pinch strength, and linear regression examined relationships between strength, ball velocity, and elbow torque (α = 0.05).
RESULTS: Dominant arm grip strength was greater than the non-dominant throwing arm (P = .001), while pinch strength showed no side to side differences (P = .696). Dominant grip strength demonstrated weak associations with height (r2 = 0.221, P = .002), weight (r2 = 0.217, P = .002), and ball velocity (r2 = 0.116, P = .021). No significant relationships were found between grip strength and elbow varus torque. Pinch strength was not associated with height, weight, age, elbow varus torque, or ball velocity.
DISCUSSION: While forearm musculature is thought to enhance medial elbow stability, grip and pinch strength were not associated with elbow varus torque in high school pitchers. These results suggest that static hand strength measures may not reflect the complex, dynamic demands placed on the elbow during pitching. Further evaluation may be necessary to determine secondary impact such as load and subsequent fatigue on the flexor pronator complex.
CONCLUSION: Grip and pinch strength values in high school pitchers may serve as reference data for clinicians assessing adolescent pitchers. Grip strength demonstrated a weak association with ball velocity; however, neither grip nor pinch strength was significantly related to elbow loading. This highlights the need for future work examining dynamic forearm muscle function in injury risk, recovery, and performance.

title: Meniscal Root Tears: Epidemiology, Diagnosis, Management, and Outcomes.
abstract: ➢ Meniscal root tears compromise load distribution within the knee, accelerating cartilage degeneration and leading to knee osteoarthritis.➢ Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion supported by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), with arthroscopy serving as the gold standard for confirmation.➢ Management decisions should be tailored to patient-specific factors, including age, activity level, tear characteristics, and the severity of degenerative chondral wear evident on preoperative imaging, including weight-bearing radiographs and MRI.➢ Root repair is associated with better long-term outcomes compared with partial meniscectomy and nonoperative management in appropriately selected patients.➢ There is currently no universally accepted postoperative rehabilitation protocol following meniscal root repair; however, most strategies limit weight-bearing in the early postoperative period and restrict loaded flexion, such as deep squatting, for up to 4 to 5 months. Further research is needed to guide standardized recovery pathways.

title: Macrophages in rotator cuff injuries and tendon-to-bone healing: Heterogeneity, pathophysiology, and therapeutic strategies.
abstract: Rotator cuff tears (RCTs) are a leading cause of shoulder disability, with high postoperative failure rates primarily attributed to poor tendon-to-bone healing. Macrophages act as central regulators of the inflammatory and regenerative microenvironment in the injured enthesis, tendon stump, subacromial bursa, and rotator cuff musculature. This review highlights the spatiotemporal heterogeneity and phenotypic plasticity of macrophages revealed by single-cell and spatial transcriptomics. Rather than following a simple M1-to-M2 transition, macrophages adopt context-dependent inflammatory, resolving, remodeling, and profibrotic programs across different stages and tissue compartments of rotator cuff injury. Persistent inflammatory programs are associated with chronic inflammation, matrix degradation, fatty infiltration, and muscle atrophy, whereas resolving and reparative programs may support inflammation resolution and fibrocartilaginous regeneration; sustained remodeling or profibrotic states may also contribute to pathological fibrosis. The review further explores macrophage-stem cell crosstalk under mechanical loading and the contribution of dysregulated macrophage function to the progression of cuff tear arthropathy. Advanced strategies including stem cell-derived exosomes, immuno-engineered scaffolds, and targeted immunomodulation, have shown therapeutic potential in preclinical studies, but their clinical efficacy and translational applicability remain to be established.

title: Adipose-Derived Orthobiologics and Extracellular Vesicles in Foot and Ankle Surgery: Current Evidence and Clinical Limitations.
abstract: Interest in adipose-derived orthobiologics and extracellular vesicles (EVs) has expanded as clinicians seek minimally invasive treatments for musculoskeletal disorders. However, culture-expanded adipose-derived stromal cells, stromal vascular fraction, microfragmented adipose tissue (MFAT), and isolated EVs are biologically and regulatorily distinct products. This narrative review summarizes their biological rationale, processing, clinical evidence, regulatory considerations, and potential application in foot and ankle surgery. Randomized studies in knee osteoarthritis suggest that MFAT may provide symptomatic improvement, but it has not consistently demonstrated superiority over other orthobiologic injections, and the certainty of evidence remains low. Preclinical EV studies provide biological plausibility for effects on tendon healing, tendon-to-bone integration, and cartilage repair. However, substantial heterogeneity in cellular source, preparation, dose, and experimental model limits translation. Human orthopaedic EV evidence remains confined to early studies in knee osteoarthritis using placental or umbilical cord derived products, with limited and conflicting evidence of efficacy and no completed studies specific to the foot and ankle. No adipose-derived regenerative medicine or EV product is Food and Drug Administration-approved for an orthopaedic indication. Current evidence therefore does not support routine clinical use or claims of tissue regeneration. Standardized product characterization and well-designed comparative trials are required to establish safety, efficacy, and appropriate clinical applications.

title: Stem cell senescence as a regenerative bottleneck in age-related skeletal degeneration: Mechanistic crosstalk and translational strategies.
abstract: Skeletal degeneration is a major cause of pain, disability, fragility fracture, and loss of independence in aging populations. Although osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, and intervertebral disc degeneration are usually managed as anatomically separate disorders, they share a common regenerative failure: endogenous stem and progenitor cells lose renewal capacity, acquire inflammatory secretory programs, and become less able to rebuild damaged matrix. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on senescence in bone marrow mesenchymal stem/stromal cells, skeletal stem cells, hematopoietic stem cells, cartilage progenitor cells, synovial mesenchymal stromal cells, and disc-derived progenitor populations. Priority is given to primary mechanistic, omics, translational, and early clinical studies that connect senescence markers with functional impairment or intervention response. We discuss telomere-associated DNA damage, mitochondrial and oxidative stress, nutrient- and mechanosensing pathways, epigenetic remodeling, dysregulated autophagy and mitophagy, and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype as interlocking mechanisms that reshape skeletal niches. Disease-specific sections then examine how senescent progenitor compartments drive osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, and intervertebral disc degeneration through impaired osteogenesis or chondrogenesis, matrix catabolism, inflammatory vesicle signaling, and maladaptive mechanical feedback. Finally, we compare senolytics, senomorphics, metabolic and mitochondrial regulators, cell rejuvenation, extracellular vesicle engineering, biomaterials, and gene-based delivery platforms from a regenerative medicine perspective. Stem/progenitor cell senescence should be treated not simply as a biomarker of aging, but as a compartment-specific therapeutic bottleneck. Translation will require rigorous cell identity, multi-parameter senescence assays, disease-stage stratification, and therapies that restore regenerative competence without suppressing physiological repair.

title: From pathogenic to reparative: Context-Dependent function of extracellular vesicles in osteoarthritis.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a whole-joint disease characterized by progressive structural degeneration and chronic low-grade inflammation affecting the cartilage, synovium, subchondral bone, and immune compartments. It is a complex degenerative disorder associated with substantial morbidity, heterogeneous clinical trajectories, and limited disease-modifying treatment options. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) have emerged as important mediators of intercellular communication within the OA joint microenvironment, and are implicated in pathophysiological responses to mechanical stress, inflammatory cues, and metabolic dysfunction. Through the transfer of context-dependent nucleic acid, protein, and lipid cargoes, EVs can amplify pathogenic processes in OA such as synovitis, cartilage catabolism, and cellular senescence, while also supporting reparative pathways. Understanding the mechanisms governing EV biogenesis, cargo selection, tissue targeting, and functional heterogeneity offers opportunities to identify mechanistically informed biomarkers and therapeutic strategies. This review discusses emerging concepts in EV-mediated joint communication, highlights translational potential and limitations, and outlines key priorities for advancing EV-based diagnostics and therapies in OA. However, EV-based strategies remain largely at the preclinical or experimental stage, and rigorous validation is required before they can enter routine clinical practice.

title: Music-based emotional regulation and nutrition strategies for mental health support among medical student-athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Medical student-athletes face combined academic, clinical, and competitive training demands that may disrupt sleep, dietary routines, emotional regulation, recovery, and cognitive functioning.
OBJECTIVE: To examine associations between naturally occurring music-based emotional regulation, self-selected nutrition routines, psychophysiological recovery, and mental health-related markers using a non-interventional multimodal digital phenotyping framework.
METHODS: Over 8 weeks, 120 medical student-athletes were monitored without prescribed music, diet, therapy, or behavioral intervention. Data included wearable-derived nocturnal heart-rate variability, resting heart rate, sleep-wake rhythm, activity and training load, participant-recorded music use, meal timing, hydration routines, food-photo logs, and brief emotional reflections. Three indices were constructed: The Music Regulation Pattern Index, Nutrition Rhythm Stability Index, and Psychophysiological Recovery Balance Index.
RESULTS: Monitoring feasibility was high and index reliability was acceptable. Music-regulation patterns were more strongly associated with emotional balance and focus-related language, whereas nutrition-rhythm stability was more closely associated with sleep regularity, heart-rate variability stability, and recovery balance.
CONCLUSION: Naturally occurring music-use and nutrition-rhythm behaviors showed distinct associations with emotional and physiological recovery markers. Multimodal digital phenotyping may help identify potentially protective lifestyle patterns in medical student-athletes while preserving an observational, non-causal interpretation and avoiding unsupported treatment claims.

title: An Intensified Training Period Reduces REM Sleep but this Decline Can Be Mitigated by Ketone Ester Supplementation.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: We previously showed that a strenuous training day disrupts sleep efficiency and REM sleep, and that these disturbances can be counteracted by ketone monoester (R)-3-hydroxybutyl-(R)-3-hydroxybutyrate (KE) supplementation. However, the impact of prolonged intensified training on sleep quality, as well as the potential modulating effect of KE are unknown.
METHODS: We performed a double-blind study in which twenty-four trained male athletes completed a 7-week training program with a gradual increase in training load while receiving either 25g of a control drink (CON, n=12) or 25g of KE (n=12) after each training session and 30 minutes before sleep. At the start (PRE), week 3 (MID), and the end (POST) of the training program, we evaluated sleep using polysomnography, and perceived stress/recovery balance using the REST-Q questionnaire. Timing, duration, and relative intensity of exercise on each testing day were identical.
RESULTS: The progressive increase in training load induced a decrease in the perceived stress-recovery state in both groups (PRE: 73±21 vs. POST: 40±37, p<0.001, Hedges' g = 1.097). From PRE to MID, sleep efficiency improved by 3% in both groups (p=0.003, Hedges' g = 0.663) while wakefulness after sleep onset reduced by 2% (p=0.031, Hedges' g = 0.716). However, from PRE to POST, total REM sleep decreased by 2% in CON but increased by 3% in KE (p=0.002, for KE vs. CON, Hedges' g = 0.939). Perceived sleep quality did not differ between groups throughout the intervention.
CONCLUSIONS: Our data indicate that KE supplementation did not enhance the beneficial effect of an initial increase in training load on sleep but prevented the decline in REM sleep upon a further training load increment.

title: The effect of positive emotions on psychophysiological recovery and performance in athletes - investigating the undoing-hypothesis.
abstract: Athletes have to cope with psychosocial and physiological stressors, requiring recovery to ensure subsequent performance. According to the undoing-hypothesis, positive emotions (PE) may enhance psychophysiological recovery. The present two studies investigated the undoing hypothesis and its benefits for athletes' cognitive (Study 1; n = 60) and motor (Study 2; n = 30) performance. After a combined psychosocial-physiological stressor, participants either completed a five-minute PE induction (music; imagination exercise) or were assigned to a resting condition. Emotions, perceived stress-recovery, and physiological parameters (e.g., heart rate, heart rate variability, cortisol) were assessed. In Study 1, inhibition and cognitive flexibility were measured once. In Study 2, hand force and jump height were measured using a pre-posttest design. Due to the lack of psychological stress responses and successful PE induction, no conclusions could be drawn regarding the undoing hypothesis. Nevertheless, the present study provides valuable methodological insights into the challenges of testing the undoing hypothesis in athletes. These insights can inform the design and implementation of future studies and thereby contribute to advancing research on the undoing hypothesis in athletic populations.

title: Resistance-trained young men exhibit enhanced carotid vasoreactivity during the cold pressor test.
abstract: The function of the common carotid artery (CCA) is integral to the regulation of cerebral perfusion. Although endurance training is associated with consistent vascular benefits, the effects of resistance training on CCA function are unclear. The cold pressor test (CPT) assesses CCA vasoreactivity via sympathetic stimulation, with peak CCA vasoreactivity (CAR%peak) reflecting integrated endothelial-autonomic vascular function. In this study, we compared CAR%peak during the CPT in resistance-trained and untrained young men and examined associations with CCA stiffness and haemodynamics. CCA ultrasound was performed in 10 resistance-trained [24 years (95% confidence interval: 22,26)] and 10 untrained [24 years (22,25)] men at baseline, during a 3-min CPT and after recovery, with simultaneous haemodynamic assessment via finger plethysmography. CAR%peak was defined as the maximal percentage increase in mean diameter from baseline. Secondary outcomes included CCA stiffness indices and haemodynamics. Both groups exhibited CCA vasodilatation during CPT; however, CAR%peak was greater in resistance-trained men (P = 0.046). The resistance-trained group also displayed greater increases in systolic diameter at end-CPT (P = 0.033), alongside attenuated pulse pressure (P = 0.050; η2 p = 0.201) and β1-stiffness (P = 0.041) responses during CPT. CAR%peak was negatively correlated with baseline β2-stiffness in resistance-trained men (r = -0.655; P = 0.040), whereas in untrained control subjects it was positively correlated with peak pulse pressure (r = 0.677; P = 0.031). In conclusion, resistance-trained young men exhibit enhanced CCA vasoreactivity and attenuated pulse pressure and stiffness responses to sympathetic stimulation, reflecting favourable adaptations in endothelial-autonomic vascular regulation. These findings highlight the potential of resistance training to improve central vascular function in early adulthood.

title: Central and peripheral vascular recovery following resistance exercise with and without blood flow restriction across age groups: a parallel group crossover randomized trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: High-intensity resistance training (HIRT) benefits musculoskeletal and vascular health but may be poorly tolerated by older adults. Low-intensity resistance training (LIRT) is an alternative, yet evidence on arterial stiffness is mixed, and it often fails to improve vascular health due to insufficient stimulus. Blood flow restriction (BFR) enhances hemodynamic stimulus, but its acute cardiovascular effects in older adults remain unclear.
PURPOSE: To compare central and peripheral vascular responses following acute LIRT with BFR versus HIRT across age groups.
METHODS: In a randomized crossover design, 19 young (22±3 years) and 19 older (70±9 years) adults completed three sessions: HIRT (3 × 10 reps at 75%1RM), LIRT+BFR (4 × 20 reps at 30%1RM with continuous cuff occlusion), and no exercise. Central and peripheral vascular function were assessed via oscillometric pulse wave analysis at rest, 5-min (RECOV1), and 30-min (RECOV2) post-exercise.
RESULTS: In older adults, neither HIRT nor LIRT+BFR altered total peripheral resistance (TPR), aortic reservoir function, or subendocardial viability ratio (SEVR) throughout post-exercise, with no differences observed between conditions. Conversely, young adults exhibited reductions at RECOV1 following HIRT in TPR (Δ = - 0.176 PRU), reservoir function (Δ = - 11.9%), and SEVR (Δ = - 47.1%), persisting at RECOV2 (all p < 0.05). LIRT+BFR elicited minor changes. Most variables normalized within 30 min for both groups.
CONCLUSION: In older adults, LIRT+BFR elicits post acute central vascular responses comparable to HIRT, with stable coronary perfusion and rapid recovery supporting the short-term tolerability of both modalities. LIRT+BFR thus represents a viable alternative to HIRT for older population.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov (ID: NCT06596304).

title: Error Related Negativity and Error Positivity: Neural Indices of Double-Faults in Elite Athletes.
abstract: ObjectiveError-related negativity (ERN) and error positivity (Pe) are key neural responses of human error monitoring. However, their relationship to behavioral adjustments after the mistakes in speeded laboratory experiments has shown mixed results. The present study examined whether ERN and Pe amplitudes would be better predictors of performance recovery following an error in a sport context than in a speeded laboratory task.MethodsFifteen male professional basketball players (18-26 years) performed a letter-based Eriksen Flanker task while their brain activity was recorded using 32-channel electroencephalography (EEG). Then, they completed a standardized 100-shot free-throw protocol on their home court. Recovery in the laboratory was measured as the ratio of back-to-back errors to total errors in the Flanker task, while recovery on the court was measured as the ratio of consecutive missed free throws to total misses. Pearson correlations and linear regression analysis were used to examine how ERP magnitudes relate to each recovery measure.ResultsAlthough ERN and Pe amplitudes were not associated with the laboratory consecutive-error ratio (all p values >.05), they were significant predictors of the field consecutive-miss ratio. Athletes with larger Pe and ERN amplitudes had significantly fewer consecutive misses (p < .001 and p = .017).ConclusionsERN and Pe may be less relevant for predicting specific post-error adjustments to immediate task demands and more relevant for predicting overall regulatory capacity in ecologically valid settings. Our findings highlight the need to use real-world performance measures when linking error monitoring with the realm of athletic performance.

title: Micro-recovery dosing in elite sport: an initiative-taking, organization-wide recovery framework.
abstract: Recovery in elite professional sport is now widely understood as a multidimensional process spanning physiological, psychological, cognitive, and social domains, yet recovery models applied in professional clubs and sporting organisations have been slow to reflect this. Most remain reactive and athlete-centred, leaving the full complexity of competitive fatigue inadequately addressed and the equivalent recovery demands on coaching and performance staff entirely unrecognised. No structural framework currently places initiative-taking, calendar-embedded multidimensional recovery as a deliberate component of seasonal planning. Main body. We introduce micro-recovery dosing (MRD): proactively planned, pre-scheduled 36-hour multidimensional recovery periods embedded within the competitive season as a proposed starting point at five to eight instances per year, extending to all members of the high-performance organisation. Drawing on neuromuscular recovery kinetics, autonomic science, sleep architecture research, occupational recovery psychology, and complex systems theory, we construct a convergent theoretical rationale for the proposed parameters and distinguish MRD from related constructs. We present a role-differentiated implementation framework with supporting evidence and a discussion of emerging AI-driven monitoring tools. Conclusions. Taken together, the four-domain convergent rationale and the complex systems perspective provide a theoretically coherent basis for MRD's proposed structure. We argue for a specific organisational transformation: the shift from recovery as an incidental gap between performance demands to an intentionally designed recovery architecture that encompasses athletes and staff alike. The article identifies the active ingredient problem as the central scientific challenge and sets out a structured empirical agenda.

title: Quantitative Muscle MRI Fat Fraction as a Biomarker of Disease Severity in Mitochondrial Myopathies.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Quantitative muscle MRI is increasingly used to assess structural muscle damage in inherited myopathies, but its application in primary mitochondrial myopathies (PMM) has not been systematically evaluated in large cohorts. Because PMM are clinically and genetically heterogeneous, objective imaging biomarkers are needed to quantify skeletal-muscle involvement and define meaningful subgroups. We assessed whether MRI-derived proton density fat fraction (PDFF) captures genotype- and phenotype-specific patterns of fatty replacement and reflects disease severity using motor function outcomes and circulating biomarkers.
METHODS: We performed a cross-sectional analysis of 49 adults with genetically confirmed PMM enrolled in a prospective natural history study. Participants underwent standardised lower-limb MRI, including T1-weighted sequences and mDIXON-QUANT fat fraction imaging. Muscle involvement was assessed semi-quantitatively with the modified Mercuri scale and quantitatively by PDFF measurement in selected pelvic girdle and thigh muscles. A total fat fraction score (FF sum) was calculated. PDFF was compared across genotypes and phenotypes and against MRC score, NSAA, 6-min walk test, 100-m run test, CK, serum creatinine, GDF15 and disease duration.
RESULTS: Mean age at onset was 26.3 ± 15.1 years, mean age at MRI was 50.0 ± 12.3 years, and median disease duration was 23 years (IQR 15-31). Genetic diagnoses included mtDNA variants in 29 patients (59.1%; single large-scale deletions, n = 19; point mutations, n = 10), nuclear variants in POLG (n = 8), TK2 (n = 8) and TWNK (n = 4). Phenotypes were exercise intolerance without overt weakness (n = 7), isolated progressive external ophthalmoplegia (PEO; n = 16), PEO-plus (n = 16) and progressive myopathy (n = 8). Highest median PDFF values were observed in tensor fasciae latae (31%), gluteus maximus (30%), sartorius (25%) and gracilis (20%). FF sum correlated with MRC score (r = -0.567, p < 0.0001), NSAA (r = -0.731, p < 0.0001), 100-m run test time (r = 0.629, p < 0.0001), 6-min walk distance (r = -0.311, p = 0.0476) and serum creatinine (r = -0.715, p < 0.0001), but not with CK or GDF15. TK2 deficiency showed the highest fat replacement, particularly in gluteus maximus and gracilis (p < 0.001). Progressive myopathy showed greater fatty replacement than other phenotypes (p < 0.001), while exercise intolerance showed higher fat fraction than isolated PEO (p = 0.033).
CONCLUSIONS: Quantitative muscle MRI provides objective and clinically meaningful measures of muscle involvement in PMM. MRI-derived fat fraction reflects disease severity, discriminates between genotypes and phenotypes, and detects subclinical muscle damage. These cross-sectional findings support PDFF as a candidate imaging biomarker for patient stratification and disease characterisation; prospective longitudinal studies will be required to establish its sensitivity to change and its validity as an outcome measure for therapeutic trials.

title: Biomimetic bilayer electrospun membrane simulating periodontal complex for orchestrated bone and fibrous tissue regeneration.
abstract: Guided tissue regeneration (GTR) is the core therapeutic strategy for repairing periodontal hard and soft tissue defects induced by periodontitis. Nevertheless, most current barrier membranes focus solely on alveolar bone reconstruction while ignoring the precise remodeling of the ordered periodontal ligament (PDL) microstructure, which impedes the integrated regeneration of functional periodontal tissues. To overcome these limitations, this study fabricated a novel bilayer composite GTR membrane with differentiated structural designs via sequential electrospinning for the synergistic and biomimetic regeneration of periodontal hard and soft tissues. The functionally graded membrane consisted of a dense, oriented poly-(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) nanofiber outer layer and a porous collagen inner layer incorporated with hydroxyapatite/β-tricalcium phosphate (HA/β-TCP) biphasic nanoparticles. The collagen matrix containing 60% HA and 40% β-TCP exhibited favorable mechanical properties that satisfy the mechanical requirements for periodontal repair. The dense PLGA layer effectively blocked the infiltration of human gingival fibroblasts (HGFs), and its physical barrier property could separate the external epithelial and connective tissues from the underlying bone tissue, offering a promising basis for the remodeling of periodontal hard and soft tissue. The inner Col/60% HA/40% β-TCP composite mimicked the natural organic-inorganic bone microenvironment and markedly promoted the adhesion, proliferation, and osteogenic differentiation of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells. The distinctive fibrous topography of the electrospun bilayer membrane provides contact guidance at the defect margins, facilitating the ordered regeneration and rearrangement of the periodontal ligament. In vivo rat periodontal defect experiments demonstrated that the bilayer membrane, compared with single-component membranes and commercial Bio-Gide membranes, significantly enhanced new bone formation and promoted the regeneration of ordered PDL-like fibrous structures with an orientation angle approaching that of the native periodontal ligament, achieving synchronized biomimetic regeneration of periodontal hard and soft tissues. In conclusion, this bilayer GTR membrane addresses the limited PDL reconstruction achieved by conventional barrier materials and provides a promising strategy for the targeted repair of complex periodontal defects.

title: Association of sleep efficiency with cardiac autonomic modulation in young and professional soccer players during pre-season.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study investigated the association between sleep efficiency and cardiac autonomic modulation in young and professional soccer players during pre-season.
METHODS: A cross-sectional quantitative study was conducted with 53 male soccer players divided into three categories: U-15 (n = 12), U-17 (n = 15), and professionals (n = 26). Sleep quality was assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), cardiac autonomic modulation via heart rate variability (HRV) recorded by a 10-lead electrocardiograph and analyzed with Kubios HRV 2.0, and cardiorespiratory capacity estimated through the Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test. Body composition was assessed by tetrapolar electrical bioimpedance. Statistical analyses included one-way ANOVA, Welch's ANOVA, chi-square and Fisher's exact tests, Pearson correlation, and simple linear regression, with significance set at p < 0.05.
RESULTS: Professional athletes demonstrated significantly higher VO₂max (50.5 ± 4.56 ml·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹; p < 0.001), lower resting heart rate (54.9 ± 8.65 bpm; p = 0.03), and greater parasympathetic modulation (RMSSD: 82.8 ± 17.5 ms; p < 0.001) compared to youth categories. Sleep efficiency was significantly higher in professionals (90.7 ± 6.13%; p = 0.01) and positively correlated with RMSSD. A significant association was found between RMSSD levels and global sleep quality (p = 0.004; X² = 0.50), as well as between RMSSD and VO₂max classification (p = 0.01; X² = 0.40).
CONCLUSION: Sleep efficiency is positively associated with cardiac autonomic modulation and aerobic performance in soccer players. While the superior physiological profile of professionals reflects a synergy between training adaptations and biological maturation, HRV and PSQI constitute complementary monitoring tools for integrated athlete assessment across competitive categories.

title: Improving sleep monitoring in athletes: a comparative evaluation of four automated sleep scoring algorithms on 204 polysomnography recordings.
abstract: ObjectiveWith advancements in AI, automated sleep scoring offers the potential for fast, precise, and cost-effective analysis. This study aimed to evaluate the accuracy, robustness, and clinical agreement of four algorithms compared to manual PSG in athletes to determine their suitability for real-life use.ApproachData from 75 athletes (204 polysomnography recordings) were retrospectively collected from studies conducted in our laboratory. Manual scoring was compared to four automated sleep staging algorithms: Luna, U-Sleep, YASA, and GSSC. Performance was evaluated based on accuracy (per stage, macro and weighted F1), sensitivity (confusion matrices), robustness (signal quality: R 2 ; individual differences: beta coefficients) and clinical relevance (prediction of total sleep time, sleep onset latency and wake after sleep onset).Main resultsAll algorithms demonstrated strong agreement with manual scoring, with macro F1 scores of 0.76 (GSSC), 0.71 (U-Sleep), 0.70 (YASA), and 0.69 (Luna). GSSC was the most accurate and robust across sport, physiological, behavioral, and anthropometric variables. It also reliably predicted total sleep time, sleep onset latency and wake after sleep onset, showing minimal bias and narrow limits of agreement. GSSC and Luna were the most resilient to signal degradation (R² = 0.08), compared to YASA (R² = 0.16) and U-Sleep (R² = 0.29).SignificanceAutomated sleep staging algorithms demonstrated accuracy comparable to typical inter-rater agreement, supporting their broader use in athletes. GSSC emerged as the most accurate and robust option, particularly resilient to signal quality degradation, a common challenge in ecological sport settings. By reducing scoring time and removing the need for expert raters, these algorithms could make polysomnography more accessible for both routine sleep monitoring and large-scale research, enabling more individualized recovery strategies and deeper insights into how sleep architecture influences athletic performance.

title: Evidence for the Effectiveness of the Performance Passport Within an Intelligence-Based Weightlifting Anti-Doping Programme.
abstract: Anti-doping organisations are tasked with detecting, deterring and preventing doping in sport, and because biological testing consumes a large share of budgets, efficient resource allocation is essential. Enhancing effectiveness requires better insight into how well current methods identify athletes at risk. The International Testing Agency (ITA) recently introduced the Athlete Performance Passport (APP), which uses competition performance data to flag at-risk weightlifters for targeted testing. This study evaluates the APP alongside established approaches, including Athlete Passport Management Unit (APMU) recommendations and atypical findings from the steroidal module of the Athlete Biological Passport (ABP). Data from 1960 male and 1583 female athletes were analysed, identifying 175 individuals (109 male and 66 female) who committed an Article 2.1 Anti-Doping Rule Violation (ADRV) between December 2009 and April 2025. The study assessed how effectively each method identified these athletes. Overall, the APP detected 34% of athletes who committed ADRVs during this period. Focusing on data since the steroidal passport's introduction in 2014, the APP identified 30% of ADRVs, outperforming APMU suspicious reports (17%) and atypical ABP steroidal profiles (10%). When combined, these methods identified 38% of ADRVs. These findings indicate that performance-based monitoring can strengthen anti-doping risk assessment and improve targeted testing strategies, particularly in sports with comprehensive competition data.

title: Bone biomarker and inflammatory cytokine responses to short-term low energy availability with and without preserved protein intake: a randomized, controlled, multi-period, cross-over trial.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Bone appears sensitive to low energy availability (LEA), with prolonged exposure linked to compromised bone health. Causality, however, along with underlying mechanisms, and the role of macronutrient availability remain unclear.
PURPOSE: To investigate the influence of short-term energy and protein manipulation on bone biomarker and inflammatory cytokine responses to acute exercise.
METHODS: Nineteen healthy, active young adults (9 females, 10 males) completed three 5-day dietary conditions in a randomized crossover design: adequate energy availability (AEA; 45 kcal·kgFFM·day-1), LEA (15 kcal·kgFFM·day-1) and LEA with protein matched to AEA (LEA-P). On days 1 and 5, participants completed a standardized exercise protocol comprising 45 min of cycling at 65% of pre-defined peak power output followed by a Wingate test, with blood samples collected at prespecified time-points to assess fasted and post-exercise bone biomarker and inflammatory cytokine responses.
RESULTS: Fasted P1NP was lower following both energy-restricted trials compared with AEA, and remained lower during post-exercise recovery following LEA-P. CTX-1 was higher in the post-exercise recovery period following LEA-P only. Multiple inflammatory cytokines (IL6, IL8, IL10, ILRa, and IL1β) increased at distinct time-points in both energy-restricted trials. Overall, evidence for condition effects relative to AEA was more consistent following LEA-P than LEA.
CONCLUSION: Short-term energy restriction suppressed biomarkers indicative of bone formation and augmented the inflammatory cytokine response to exercise, with some, but less consistent evidence for increased bone resorption. Preserving protein intake did not attenuate these effects. In contrast, this condition was associated with more consistent and pronounced perturbations, potentially reflecting reduced carbohydrate availability rather than protein per se.

title: Combined anterior cruciate ligament and anterolateral ligament reconstruction leads to better postural control than isolated anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in the early postoperative phase.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Recent studies suggest that the anterolateral ligament (ALL) contributes to knee rotational stability by acting synergistically with the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). Although combined ACL and ALL reconstruction has shown benefits in physical examination, subjective physical scales, and return-to-sport or re-rupture rates, few studies have compared postural control. This study aimed to compare postural control between isolated ACL reconstruction and combined ACL and ALL reconstruction.
METHODS: Between June 2016 and July 2022, patients who underwent isolated ACL reconstruction (n = 37) or combined ACL and ALL reconstruction (n = 30) were included. Static and dynamic postural control were assessed using the Biodex Balance System and the Y-balance test (YBT) preoperatively and at three and six months postoperatively.
FINDINGS: A total of 67 patients were enrolled, including 49 men and 18 women, with a mean age of 30.2 ± 8.1 years and a mean body mass index of 25.98 ± 3.6 kg/m2. In the YBT, which assesses dynamic postural control as the contralateral limb moves away from the center of gravity, significant main effects of time and group were observed, except in the anterior direction. The YBT-posteromedial (p = 0.009) and YBT-posterolateral (p = 0.049) directions, which reflect knee rotational stability, was significantly better in the combined ACL and ALL reconstruction group than in the isolated ACL reconstruction group.
INTERPRETATION: At three months postoperatively, combined ACL and ALL reconstruction showed better dynamic postural control than isolated ACL reconstruction, particularly during tasks requiring multidirectional postural adjustments.

title: Concussion symptom clusters and changes in symptom reporting and severity following multiple concussions in male professional rugby league players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Symptom reporting remains an important part of the diagnosis and management of concussion. Understanding the patterns of symptoms and symptom clusters in athletes with multiple concussions may be clinically valuable. The purpose of this study was to characterise acute symptom reporting in players with multiple concussions.
METHODS: National Rugby League (NRL) players who have sustained multiple concussions between the 2017 and 2022 seasons were included in the study. Data included the symptoms reported on the Sport Concussion Assessment Tool - 5th Edition (SCAT5) during the Head Injury Assessment by players who were subsequently diagnosed with concussion. K-means clustering with k = 6 centres was performed on symptom severity data. Each concussion episode was assigned to one symptom cluster based on the athlete's symptom presentation. Transitions between symptom clusters from initial to subsequent concussions were visualised using a Sankey plot.
RESULTS: There were 120 players who sustained more than one concussion, including 75 players with two, 23 with three, 15 with four, and 7 players with five or more medically diagnosed concussions. The average duration between concussions was 441 days (SD: 332; Md: 370; range: 11-1435 days). There were 6 different symptom clusters identified. Players were commonly found to transition between clusters for subsequent concussions, most commonly the 'Asymptomatic' cluster. There was no relationship found for days between concussions and symptom count or severity. Symptom severity, but not symptom count, was associated with days until medical clearance.
CONCLUSION: Acute symptom reporting varies with subsequent concussions, making it difficult to predict post-concussion symptoms in individual players. Acute symptom severity was associated with time to medical clearance, whereas the number of concussions in the preceding two years was not.

title: The role of plantar flexor function, isometric strength and task-specific kinetics, in sprint and jump performance.
abstract: The role of isometric plantar flexion (PF) strength in sprinting and jumping is unclear and, in part, may be due to methodological issues with isometric dynamometry leading to inaccurate measures of PF strength. In addition, the relationship, and thus functional relevance, of isometric PF strength with PF kinetics during these athletic tasks remains unknown. The aim of this study was to assess the interrelationships of isometric PF strength, task-specific sprint and jump PF kinetics and overall performance during jumps and sprint acceleration. Three-dimensional kinematics and ground reaction forces were recorded in 38 healthy individuals of varying athletic ability (18 females; height 1.75 ± 0.09 m; Mass: 70.9 ± 10.0 kg, Age 23 ± 3 years) during: standing isometric PF dynamometry, countermovement jumps (CMJ), drop jumps (DJ) and sprints. Isometric PF strength and sprint/jump PF kinetics were both assessed via inverse dynamics. Sprint speed, CMJ height and DJ reactive strength index defined task performances. Specific sprint and jump PF kinetics showed moderate-large correlations to task performances in 7 out of 9 relationships with peak positive power explaining 19-50% of the variance in the performance of these tasks (r/ρ = 0.434-0.706; p ≤ 0.024). Isometric PF strength, however, was unrelated to performance (CMJ: r = 0.126, DJ: r = 0.301, Sprint: ρ = 0.142), or task-specific PF kinetics during sprinting and jumping (all r ≤ 0.329). Dynamic task-specific function of the PF was an important component of overall performance, but this was not the case for isometric PF strength. These results highlight the distinctiveness of dynamic stretch-shortening cycle specific PF function compared to standing isometric PF strength for athletic performance.

title: The Effect of Training Exercise on Cartilage Zonal Composition and Structure at Two Differently Loaded Sites in the Juvenile Equine Metacarpophalangeal Joint.
abstract: BackgroundThe aim of this study was to investigate the depth related spatial distribution of biochemical and structural components in articular cartilage at different topographical sites experiencing different loading within the juvenile equine metacarpophalangeal joint in two groups of foals subjected to different exercise conditions.MethodsSixteen Warmblood foals were included in the study and were randomly assigned into 1 of 2 exercise groups (box rest and box rest plus training) during the first 5 months of life and subsequently euthanized. Osteochondral plugs were harvested from two sites which have previously been shown to experience different load levels and sectioned into 100 μm thick slices. Cartilage slices were analysed for glycosaminoglycan, DNA, and total collagen content, as well as content of hydroxylysine residues (HYL) in collagen and the collagen cross-link Hydroxylysylpyridinoline (HP). Collagen fibril architecture (Orientation Angle and Parallelism Index) was determined using quantitative polarized light microscopy.ResultsThe constantly loaded site 2 exhibited higher glycosaminoglycan (GAG) and HP content with HYL higher in the superficial and middle layers of the trained group, while the intermittently peak loaded site 1 showed greater collagen accumulation in deeper layers but lower cross-link density. Structural analyses (Oa and PI) confirmed that collagen fibril orientation and alignment adapt regionally, with training enhancing fibril organization in superficial zones.ConclusionThis study illustrates that mechanical loading is a key driver of functional adaptation, resulting in distinct zonal and topographical differences in the biochemical and structural composition of equine cartilage at 5 months.

title: A wearable vibroarthrography system with PID-controlled negative-pressure suction and synchronized posture estimation.
abstract: BackgroundVibroarthrography (VAG) is a non-invasive technique for evaluating joint health through acoustic signals generated during movement. However, reliable signal acquisition during dynamic activities remains challenging due to sensor displacement, motion artifacts, and inconsistent skin contact.ObjectiveThis study proposes an advanced wearable VAG system integrating PID-controlled negative-pressure suction and real-time posture estimation to improve signal stability and enhance the assessment of knee joint mechanics during movement.MethodsThe proposed system combines a wearable acoustic sensing module with a vacuum-assisted suction cup and a PID controller that consistently maintains sensor adhesion. Real-time posture estimation is achieved using MediaPipe Pose, which computes knee flexion angles. VAG signals and kinematic data are synchronously acquired during OKC and CKC exercises for integrated analysis.ResultsIn this single-subject pilot test, the system achieved stable sensor attachment and repeatable vibroacoustic recordings throughout dynamic movements. Distinguishable frequency-domain characteristics were observed at relevant knee flexion angles, including approximately 30°, 63°, and 129°.ConclusionsThis pilot feasibility study demonstrates that the proposed wearable VAG platform can achieve stable acquisition of synchronized vibroacoustic and kinematic signals during dynamic knee movement in a single subject. These preliminary findings suggest potential future applications in osteoarthritis screening, rehabilitation assessment, and ambulatory monitoring, pending validation in larger, statistically powered cohorts.

title: Impact of foot orthoses hindfoot and forefoot wedges on foot and ankle kinematics: A cadaveric study.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Foot orthoses (FOs) are widely prescribed to manage musculoskeletal and inflammatory disorders affecting the lower limbs by modifying foot and ankle biomechanics. While the addition of medial wedges to FOs is believed to enhance control of pronation-related movements, few studies have quantified their isolated kinematic effects under controlled experimental conditions. The use of cadaveric models allows for precise measurement of bone motion without soft tissue artifacts. Therefore, this study aimed to quantify the effects of 3D-printed FOs with and without a medial hindfoot-forefoot wedge on foot and ankle kinematics in cadaveric specimens during quasi-dynamic loading. It was hypothesized that a medial hindfoot-forefoot wedge would better prevent both forefoot dorsiflexion and ankle eversion in cadaveric specimens.
MATERIAL AND METHODS: Nine fresh-frozen lower limbs were tested under three randomized conditions: shoe-only (control), standard FOs (SFO), and medial hindfoot-forefoot wedge FOs (MWFO). FOs were 3D printed in PA11 using the multi-jet fusion technology. Specimens were mounted on a mechanical press with simulated muscle tension applied through tendon loading. Kinematic data were collected via a six-camera motion capture system and reflective markers attached to bone-anchored rods. Ankle and forefoot/hindfoot angles and ranges of motion were calculated in the sagittal, frontal, and transverse planes. Non-parametric Friedman ANOVAs and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used to assess between-condition differences (α < 0.05).
RESULTS: Compared to the control condition, MWFOs significantly reduced peak ankle dorsiflexion (1.40° ± 3.76° vs 3.54° ± 2.74°, p < 0.001) and increased ankle inversion (9.12° ± 11.13° vs 7.09° ± 11.73°, p = 0.002). MWFOs also increased forefoot/hindfoot plantarflexion (p = 0.018) and adduction (p = 0.018) relative to the control condition. No significant differences in joint range of motion were observed across conditions.
CONCLUSIONS: The addition of a hindfoot-forefoot medial wedge to 3D-printed FOs modifies ankle and midfoot kinematics under quasi-dynamic loading, primarily by reducing pronation-related movements such as dorsiflexion and eversion. These findings support the biomechanical rationale for incorporating hindfoot-forefoot medial wedges in FOs design to enhance control of foot and ankle motion.

title: Camera-Based AI-Assisted Scoring for the Balance Error Scoring System: A Cross-sectional Validity and Agreement Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The Balance Error Scoring System (BESS) is widely used to assess static postural control in sports medicine and rehabilitation. However, conventional real-time scoring is observer dependent and may be influenced by rater experience, viewing angle, attention, and the interpretation of transient or overlapping errors. This study evaluated the criterion-related validity and agreement of a camera-based artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted BESS relative to consensus video-review manual scoring and compared its error magnitude with on-site manual scoring.
METHODS: This single-center cross-sectional study included 80 of 84 recruited participants: 40 healthy controls, 20 with chronic ankle instability (CAI), and 20 after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR). All participants completed the standard six-condition BESS protocol. Scores were obtained using AI-assisted, on-site manual, and consensus video-review manual scoring; the latter was prespecified as the pragmatic manual reference standard. Primary total-score analyses included Pearson correlation, the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), Bland-Altman mean difference and 95% limits of agreement (LoA), mean absolute error (MAE), and root mean square error (RMSE). Condition- and group-specific analyses were exploratory.
RESULTS: For the total BESS score, AI-assisted scoring versus the reference showed r = 0.989, ICC = 0.989 (95% CI 0.982-0.993), a mean difference of 0.188 errors, 95% LoA from -2.063 to 2.438 errors, an MAE of 0.787 errors, and an RMSE of 1.157 errors. On-site manual scoring versus the reference showed r = 0.922, ICC = 0.920 (95% CI 0.877-0.948), a mean difference of -0.612 errors, 95% LoA from -6.680 to 5.455 errors, an MAE of 2.212 errors, and an RMSE of 3.136 errors. Condition-specific discrepancies were larger in the single-leg and tandem-stance conditions. Exploratory group comparisons showed higher total BESS scores in individuals with CAI than in healthy controls.
CONCLUSIONS: Camera-based AI-assisted BESS scoring showed strong total-score agreement with the pragmatic manual reference standard and smaller discrepancies than on-site manual scoring. This approach may support more standardized BESS assessment; however, external validation and longitudinal reliability testing are required before interchangeability with manual scoring can be considered.

title: Heart-to-kidney signal by extracellular vesicles promotes kidney injury in cardiorenal syndrome.
abstract:
AIMS: Cardiorenal syndrome type-1 (CRS1), defined as acute kidney injury occurring in the setting of acute cardiac illness, is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Our objective was to determine whether extracellular vesicles (EVs) derived from the injured heart localize to the kidneys and contribute to renal injury in CRS1, and to elucidate mechanisms by which cardiac-derived EVs mediate kidney damage.
METHODS AND RESULTS: Using cardiomyocyte-specific EV reporter mice, we characterized the release of cardiac-derived EVs and their biodistribution to the kidneys. Acute myocardial infarction increased circulating levels of these EVs and enhanced their uptake by proximal tubular epithelial cells. To directly assess their impact on the kidney, EVs derived from cardiomyocytes cultured under normoxic (N-EV) or hypoxic (H-EV) conditions were injected into the renal arteries of wild-type mice. H-EV, but not N-EV, induced proximal tubular epithelial cell injury and worsening of kidney function. To identify EV biomarkers, we performed proteomic profiling of cargo from N-EV and H-EV, and validated the muscle-specific protein TRIM72 as a biomarker of EVs originating from injured cardiomyocytes. In a porcine CRS1 model, plasma levels of TRIM72 positive-EVs were increased, and we demonstrate their delivery to the kidney. Similarly, in CRS1 patients, higher plasma levels of TRIM72-positive EVs correlated with the development of acute kidney injury. Mechanistically, uptake of H-EVs by proximal tubular epithelial cells induced transcription of lipogenic genes and caused lipid accumulation, whereas lipogenesis blockade protected these cells from H-EV-induced injury. We subsequently found that reduced expression of the transcription factor FOXO3 drove H-EV-induced transcriptomic reprogramming. H-EV cargo was enriched with specific Foxo3-targeting miRNAs, whose delivery promoted proximal tubular epithelial cell cytotoxicity, oxidative stress, and suppressed FOXO3 levels.
CONCLUSIONS: Overall, this work demonstrates that a Foxo3-targeting miRNA heart-to-kidney signal mediated by injured cardiac-derived EVs contributes to kidney injury in CRS1.

title: Sleep-related metrics that predict training intensity: an exploratory study in women's college athletics.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: In recent years, the development of wearable monitoring technologies has expanded objective assessments of workload and fatigue, predominantly via heart rate (HR)-based markers (e.g., heart rate variability, resting heart rate). There are also perception-based markers of exertion commonly used in high-performance training settings, such as rating of perceived exertion (RPE) scales. Previous research has shown that these markers do not measure identical but rather complementary aspects of exertion, but limited data exist on the relationships between objective and subjective markers at the daily level; data which may be especially important for understanding how to best monitor for effort or overtraining. This study will characterize both HR- and perception-based markers of exertion at the daily level in women's college athletes. Additionally, given the powerful influence of sleep on both athletic performance and perceptions of physical exertion, we further explored how sleep behaviors at the within- and between-person level relate to daily assessments of subjective and objective exertion.
METHODS: Thirteen women's college athletes continuously wore a WHOOP activity monitor for this two-week observational study. RPE was self-reported within 30 min of completing a training session or competition and prior to viewing WHOOP data.
RESULTS: A series of descriptive statistics and Pearson correlation were conducted to describe the relationship between RPE and activity strain on a daily level among the population studied. A series of linear mixed-effects models demonstrated worse sleep on average (i.e., more debt, poorer sleep performance) was associated with higher HR-based markers of exertion; however, within-person elevations in sleep consistency, but more sleep need on average was associated with higher HR-based measures of exertion and lower perceptions of exertion.
CONCLUSIONS: Findings support the need for additional research to better understand the drivers of daily markers of exertion to enhance the health and performance of athletes.

title: The Influence of Menstrual Cycle Phase and Cramp Severity on Psychological Responses and Exercise Capacity in Physically Active Eumenorrheic Women.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The scientific literature is characterized by a historical underrepresentation of the female population in sports science. A critical issue in the current literature is the inconsistency between objectively measured (e.g., time to exhaustion) and subjectively perceived performance across the menstrual cycle. This inconsistency is often attributed to methodological limitations (e.g., absence of hormonal assessments and ovulation kits) and to the lack of consideration of menstrual-related symptoms and psychological variables.
PURPOSE: The primary objective of the study was to compare graded exercise test (GXT) performance outcomes across menstrual cycle phases. A secondary objective was to investigate whether cramp severity was associated with GXT performance during menses. A final objective was to examine the effects of menstrual cycle phase on psychological responses to exercise.
METHODS: Nineteen physically active eumenorrheic women (age 24 ± 4 years, V̇O2peak 38.4 ± 3.1 mL·kg -1·min -1) completed five GXTs: two for familiarization and three performed during experimental sessions scheduled in three specific phases of the menstrual cycle (menses, follicular, and luteal). Variables of interest included estradiol and progesterone levels, affective valence, arousal, anxiety, heart rate, rating of perceived exertion, mood disturbance, and motivation. Exercise capacity was operationalized as GXT performance outcomes (peak power output [Wpeak] and time to exhaustion). Cramp severity was measured only during menses.
RESULTS: No statistically significant differences in Wpeak or time to exhaustion were detected across menstrual cycle phases (p > 0.05). Secondary and exploratory regression analyses indicated that each one-point increase in menstrual cramp severity during menses was associated with lower GXT performance (Wpeak: -1.50 W; time to exhaustion: 2.72 s; p = 0.04; R 2 = ~0.35). Higher affective valence scores were associated with improved Wpeak (+4.27 W) and time to exhaustion (-8.51 s; p = 0.02; R 2 = ~0.36), whereas higher arousal scores were associated with lower Wpeak (-11.40 W) and higher time to exhaustion (6.47 s; p = 0.01; R 2 = ~0.46) across the menstrual cycle. Motivation was lower during menses than during the follicular phase (p = 0.04).
CONCLUSIONS: No statistically significant differences in GXT performance were detected across menstrual cycle phases. However, secondary and exploratory analyses suggest that greater menstrual cramp severity during menses was associated with lower time to exhaustion and Wpeak. These findings provide preliminary evidence that menstrual-related symptoms and psychological factors may contribute to variability in GXT performance outcomes and warrant further investigation in larger cohorts.

title: Using High-Field Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy to Measure Muscle Glycogen in Patients With McArdle Disease.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION/AIMS: Patients with McArdle disease demonstrate exercise intolerance with muscle contractures and episodic rhabdomyolysis. Additionally, some patients show progressive fat replacement of paraspinal and shoulder muscles with aging. The cause of fat replacement in older McArdle patients is unknown but could relate to a higher glycogen accumulation in these muscles in line with what is found in Pompe disease. The aim of the study was to investigate if this is also the case in McArdle disease, which could imply that excess levels of glycogen accumulation are a potential driver of fat replacement of muscle.
METHODS: Using 7 Tesla 13C magnetic resonance spectroscopy, we measured glycogen noninvasively in lumbar, thigh, and calf muscles in 14 patients with McArdle disease and 19 healthy controls.
RESULTS: Patients with McArdle disease showed increased levels of glycogen in all muscles compared to controls; calf (3.2 times normal, p < 0.005), hamstrings (2.7 times normal, p < 0.005), anterior thigh compartment (2.7 times normal, p < 0.005), and lumbar muscle (2.1 times normal, p < 0.005). Glycogen was evenly distributed among muscle groups in both patients with McArdle disease and healthy controls.
DISCUSSION: Our results are in line with previous studies showing two to three times increased glycogen compared to control in muscle biopsies. We found no variability in glycogen concentration among muscles that could indicate glycogen as a predictor of muscle injury in McArdle disease.
